74276.m: Discourse ethics provides a procedure, not ready-made content.

74277.q: With which school of thought is Jürgen Habermas associated as the most important representative of its second generation?
74277.e: Habermas was an assistant to Theodor W. Adorno at the Frankfurt Institute for Social Research. He developed Critical Theory further.
74277.m: Jürgen Habermas belongs to the Frankfurt School.

74278.q: According to Hans Jonas, why is traditional ethics no longer enough in the technological age?
a: It related only to near and immediate consequences of actions
It knew no duties at all
It applied only to rulers and kings
74278.e: Earlier ethics regulated dealings between contemporaries close at hand. Modern technology, however, has effects far into space and time, for example through nuclear power or interference with nature.
74278.m: According to Jonas, modern technology demands an ethics of long-range effects.

74279.q: What is the subtitle of ‘The Imperative of Responsibility’ (in German ‘Das Prinzip Verantwortung’)?
a: In Search of an Ethics for the Technological Age
Foundations of an Ethics of Compassion
A Theory of Justice for Free Citizens
Studies on the Ethics of Antiquity
74279.e: Jonas was responding to the fact that modern technology has far-reaching and long-term consequences. Traditional ethics, he said, had only looked at what was near and present.
74279.m: Jonas designed an ethics for the age of technology.

74280.q: What is Hans Jonas’s new imperative?
a: Act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life on Earth
Act so that you can defend the maxim of your action before a court at any time
Act so that as many people alive today as possible become happy
Act as you would expect a virtuous person to act
74280.e: Jonas reformulated the categorical imperative for the technological age. At its centre is the survival of humanity.
74280.m: Jonas demands that we act so that human life on Earth remains possible for ever.

74281.q: What does Jonas call the principle of taking the worst scenarios especially seriously when the consequences of technology are uncertain?
74281.e: Imagining possible disasters should help us see what is at stake. That is why the bad forecast should be given priority over the good one.
74281.m: The heuristics of fear takes possible disasters especially seriously.

74282.q: According to Jonas, towards whom do humans have a new, special responsibility?
74282.e: Future people cannot represent their own interests today. Because our technology determines their living conditions, we are responsible for them.
74282.m: Jonas stresses responsibility for future generations.

74283.q: For Hans Jonas, what is the archetype, the original image of all responsibility?
a: Parents’ responsibility for their newborn baby
A judge’s responsibility for a verdict
74283.e: The helpless newborn demands care simply by existing. Jonas uses this to show that responsibility arises from the vulnerability of the other.
74283.m: For Jonas, caring for a newborn shows the original image of responsibility.

74284.q: Which work does the German title ‘Das Prinzip Verantwortung’ (The Principle of Responsibility) allude to?
a: ‘The Principle of Hope’ by Ernst Bloch
74284.e: Ernst Bloch designed a utopian philosophy of hope. Jonas deliberately set against it an ethics of cautious responsibility.
74284.m: Jonas’s title answers Ernst Bloch’s ‘The Principle of Hope’.

74285.q: Which major prize did Hans Jonas receive in 1987?
a: The Peace Prize of the German Book Trade
The Charlemagne Prize of the city of Aachen
74285.e: With the Peace Prize, the German book trade honoured Jonas’s contribution to ethics in the technological age. Jonas was living in the USA at the time.
74285.m: Hans Jonas received the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade in 1987.

74286.q: In which year did John Rawls publish his main work ‘A Theory of Justice’?
74286.e: The book appeared in 1971 and gave political philosophy a strong revival.
74286.m: John Rawls published ‘A Theory of Justice’ in 1971.

74287.q: What does Rawls call the imagined situation in which people do not know what position they will have in society?
74287.e: Behind this veil, nobody knows their background, talents, wealth or sex. In this way fair principles are to be chosen that favour no one.
74287.m: Behind the veil of ignorance, you choose fair rules for everyone.

74288.q: In Rawls, what is the fictional starting situation in which the principles of justice are chosen called?
74288.e: The original position is a thought experiment and corresponds to the state of nature in older contract theories. The participants there are free, equal and rational.
74288.m: In the original position, free and equal people choose the principles of justice.

74289.q: With which slogan does Rawls sum up his theory of justice?
74289.e: The principles are fair because they are chosen under fair conditions. Rawls deliberately sets his theory against utilitarianism.

74290.q: What does Rawls’s difference principle state?
a: Inequalities are allowed only if they benefit the least advantaged the most
All people must own exactly the same amount
Everyone should receive what they earn on the market
Inequalities are allowed if the majority agrees
74290.e: Differences in income and wealth are justified if they also improve the position of the weakest. A doctor may earn more if this benefits everyone, including the poorest.
74290.m: For Rawls, inequality is only just if it helps the weakest.

74291.q: Which principle takes priority over all others for Rawls?
74291.e: The first principle guarantees everyone an equal system of basic liberties such as freedom of opinion and conscience. These must not be restricted for economic advantages.
74291.m: For Rawls, equal basic liberties come before economic advantages.

74292.q: According to Rawls, which decision rule do people choose in the original position?
74292.e: With the maximin rule, you choose the option whose worst outcome is the best. Anyone who does not know where they will end up protects themselves in this way against the worst lot.
74292.m: With the maximin rule, you choose the option with the best worst case.

74293.q: Which philosopher criticised Rawls from a libertarian point of view in ‘Anarchy, State, and Utopia’ in 1974?
74293.e: Robert Nozick, a colleague of Rawls at Harvard University, defended a minimal state. He saw redistribution through taxes as an interference with property rights.
74293.m: Robert Nozick criticised Rawls from a libertarian point of view.

74294.q: Which British philosopher first formulated the trolley problem in 1967?
74294.e: Philippa Foot used the example in an essay on the doctrine of double effect. Since then it has been one of the best-known thought experiments in ethics.
74294.m: Philippa Foot introduced the trolley problem in 1967.

74295.q: Who coined the name ‘trolley problem’ in 1976 and developed the thought experiment further?
74295.e: The American philosopher Judith Jarvis Thomson compared different versions of the dilemma. A well-known one is the bridge version, in which you would have to push a person onto the tracks to save five.
74295.m: Judith Jarvis Thomson gave the trolley problem its name.

74296.q: How does a utilitarian typically decide in the basic version: switch the points so that one person dies instead of five?
a: He leaves the points as they are
He refuses to answer at all
74296.e: For utilitarianism, the consequences count: one death is less bad than five. That is why switching is required.
74296.m: Utilitarians save the larger number in the trolley case.

74298.q: Why do many people consider pushing a man off a bridge more wrong than switching the points?
a: Because the man is used merely as a means
Because the train then goes faster
74298.e: When pushing, the man’s body serves directly to stop the train. With the points, his death is a side effect, not the means of rescue.
74298.m: Many reject using a person as a tool to save others.

74299.q: What is the name of MIT’s online experiment that collected millions of judgements on accident decisions by self-driving vehicles?
74299.e: The results were published in the journal ‘Nature’ in 2018. They showed that moral preferences differ in part depending on the world region.
74299.m: MIT’s Moral Machine experiment collected judgements on dilemmas of self-driving cars worldwide.

74300.q: How did the German Federal Constitutional Court rule in 2006 on permission to shoot down a hijacked passenger plane?
a: The rule is incompatible with human dignity and void
Shooting it down is allowed if more people are saved
Shooting it down is allowed only at night
Parliament alone decides in each individual case
74300.e: The court declared the shoot-down power in the Aviation Security Act unconstitutional. The passengers must not be treated as mere objects for saving others.
74300.m: In 2006 the German Constitutional Court put human dignity above weighing up victims.

74301.q: What do the 2017 guidelines of the German ethics commission on automated driving forbid in unavoidable accidents?
a: Choosing victims by personal features such as age
74301.e: Any distinction based on age, sex or physical condition is strictly forbidden. This rules out classic trolley-style weighing up of persons.
74301.m: Self-driving cars must not choose victims by personal features.

74302.q: What is the legal status of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
a: It is a resolution without binding force in international law
It is a treaty ratified by all states
It is part of the Swiss Federal Constitution
It is enforced by the UN Security Council
74302.e: The declaration was adopted as a recommendation of the UN General Assembly. Binding treaties followed later, above all the two human rights covenants of 1966.
74302.m: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is a recommendation, not a binding treaty.

74303.q: Who chaired the UN commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights?
74303.e: The former First Lady of the USA chaired the Commission on Human Rights. She worked hard for the declaration to be adopted.
74303.m: Eleanor Roosevelt led the drafting of the human rights declaration.

74304.q: Which right is counted among the so-called third generation of human rights?
a: The right to a healthy environment
The right to freedom of assembly
74304.e: The third generation includes collective solidarity rights such as the right to development, peace and a healthy environment. They often belong to peoples or groups, not only to individuals.
74304.m: The third generation includes collective rights such as the right to a healthy environment.

74305.q: Which three qualities are usually attributed to human rights?
74305.e: Human rights apply to all people, cannot be given up or taken away and are connected with one another. So they must not be played off against each other.
74305.m: Human rights are universal, inalienable and indivisible.

74306.q: Which right belongs to the economic, social and cultural human rights (second generation)?
a: The right to freedom of opinion
The right to a fair trial
74306.e: The first generation covers civil and political freedoms. The second generation requires the state to provide services, such as education, social security and health care.
74306.m: The right to education is one of the social human rights.

74307.q: In which city is the UN Human Rights Council, founded in 2006, based?
74307.e: The Human Rights Council replaced the former Commission on Human Rights in 2006. It meets in the Palais des Nations in Geneva.
74307.m: The UN Human Rights Council is based in Geneva.

74308.q: In which year did Switzerland join the two UN human rights covenants (civil and social covenant)?
74308.e: The covenants were adopted by the UN in 1966. For Switzerland they came into force in 1992, ten years before it joined the UN.
74308.m: Switzerland has been bound by the two UN human rights covenants since 1992.

74309.q: Which four principles make up the medical ethics approach of Tom Beauchamp and James Childress?
74309.e: In 1979 Beauchamp and Childress set out four mid-level principles: respect for autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence (doing good) and justice. They are to be weighed against each other in everyday clinical work.
74309.m: Principlism weighs autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence and justice against each other.

74310.q: What is the principle called that patients must freely agree to a treatment after receiving understandable information?
74310.e: Informed consent requires information, capacity to judge and voluntariness. Without it, a medical procedure counts legally as bodily harm.
74310.m: A procedure needs the free consent of a well-informed person.

74311.q: What is it called when professionals override the will of a person capable of judgement for that person’s supposed good?
74311.e: Paternalism comes from the Latin pater (father) and means a patronising kind of care. It is in tension with respect for self-determination.
74311.m: Paternalism is care that overrides self-determination.

74312.q: Which document laid down basic rules for experiments on humans in 1947 as part of the Nuremberg Doctors’ Trial?
74312.e: The Nuremberg Code was part of the verdict against Nazi doctors who had carried out cruel experiments on people. Its first point requires the voluntary consent of the test subject.
74312.m: The Nuremberg Code of 1947 made voluntary consent a condition of all research on humans.

74313.q: Which organisation adopted the Declaration of Helsinki on ethical principles for medical research in 1964?
74313.e: The Declaration of Helsinki comes from the World Medical Association and is revised regularly. It is regarded worldwide as a guideline for research on humans.
74313.m: The Declaration of Helsinki is the World Medical Association’s research ethics document.

74314.q: Which pledge of 1948 is regarded as a modern version of the Hippocratic Oath?
74314.e: The World Medical Association adopted the Declaration of Geneva in 1948 in response to the crimes of doctors under National Socialism. It has been revised several times, most recently in 2017.
74314.m: The Declaration of Geneva is the modern doctors’ oath.

74315.q: What is the sorting of patients by urgency called when treatment options are not enough for everyone?
74315.e: Triage comes from the French trier (to sort). It is ethically delicate because decisions must be made on distributing scarce resources such as intensive care beds.
74315.m: In triage, patients are sorted by urgency and chance of success.

74316.q: Which Swiss institution draws up medical ethics guidelines that are often adopted into the FMH code of conduct?
74316.e: The Swiss Academy of Medical Sciences (SAMS) publishes guidelines, for example on capacity to judge or end of life. Once included in the FMH code of conduct, they are binding for its members.
74316.m: The SAMS issues important medical ethics guidelines in Switzerland.

74317.q: Since which year has the advance directive been explicitly regulated in the Swiss Civil Code?
74317.e: With the new adult protection law, the provisions on advance directives (Art. 370 ff. Civil Code) came into force on 1 January 2013. A person capable of judgement can thus decide in advance which treatments they agree to.
74317.m: Since 2013 the Civil Code has regulated advance directives.

74318.q: Which model of organ donation did Swiss voters accept on 15 May 2022?
74318.e: With the amendment to the Transplantation Act, anyone who did not object during their lifetime is to count as a donor. Implementation needs a new register and is delayed by several years.
74318.m: Since the 2022 vote, anyone who does not object counts in principle as a donor.

74319.q: With roughly what percentage of yes votes was the amendment to the Transplantation Act accepted in May 2022?
74319.e: The proposal received about 60 per cent yes votes. This meant the referendum against the indirect counter-proposal to the organ donation initiative had failed.
74319.m: The organ donation reform was accepted in 2022 with about three fifths voting yes.

74320.q: Which rule applied in Switzerland to organ donation after death before the 2022 reform?
74320.e: Until then, organs could only be removed if the deceased person had agreed or the relatives agreed in line with their wishes. If neither was the case, no removal was allowed.
74320.m: In the past, organs could only be removed with consent.

74321.q: What does the word ‘extended’ mean in the extended opt-out system?
74321.e: If there is no documented decision, the relatives are asked. They can refuse removal if they know or assume that the person would have been against it.
74321.m: In the extended system, relatives have a say.

74322.q: According to Swiss transplantation law, which condition must be established before organs may be removed from a deceased person?
74322.e: The Transplantation Act defines death as the irreversible loss of all functions of the brain, including the brainstem. Two specialists must establish it independently.
74322.m: Organs may only be removed once brain death has been established.

74323.q: Which national foundation coordinates the allocation of donor organs in Switzerland?
74323.e: On behalf of the Confederation, Swisstransplant runs the national allocation office and keeps the waiting list. Criteria such as medical urgency and waiting time are set by law.
74323.m: Swisstransplant allocates donor organs in Switzerland.

74324.q: Which principle applies to organ donation under the Swiss Transplantation Act?
a: It must be free of charge
It is compensated by the state
74324.e: No financial gain or other advantage may be granted for donating organs, and organ trafficking is a criminal offence. Only reimbursement of costs such as loss of earnings is allowed.
74324.m: Organs may not be sold in Switzerland.

74325.q: Who performed Switzerland’s first heart transplant in Zurich in 1969?
74325.e: The Swedish surgeon Åke Senning worked at the University Hospital Zurich and carried out Switzerland’s first heart transplant in April 1969. The world’s first heart transplant had taken place in Cape Town in 1967.
74325.m: Switzerland’s first heart transplant succeeded in Zurich in 1969.

74326.q: Which organ is most often donated by living people in Switzerland?
74326.e: Because people can live well with one healthy kidney, living kidney donation is the most common form of living donation. Donating part of the liver is also possible.
74326.m: You can donate a kidney while alive.

74327.q: When is assisting suicide a criminal offence under Art. 115 of the Swiss Criminal Code?
74327.e: Art. 115 of the Criminal Code punishes anyone who, for selfish motives, incites someone to suicide or helps them, for example out of greed. Without such motives, assisted suicide is not punishable, which is what Swiss assisted dying organisations rely on.
74327.m: In Switzerland, assisted suicide is only punishable when done for selfish motives.

74328.q: Under which offence does the Swiss Criminal Code punish direct active euthanasia?
74328.e: Anyone who kills a person at their serious and insistent request is liable to punishment under Art. 114 of the Criminal Code. What matters is that another person carries out the fatal act.
74328.m: Direct active euthanasia is forbidden in Switzerland as killing on request.

74329.q: What is withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining measures called?
74329.e: In passive euthanasia, for example, ventilation or artificial feeding is ended so that the illness takes its course. It is permitted in Switzerland if it is in line with the patient’s wishes.
74329.m: Passive euthanasia means leaving out life-sustaining measures.

74330.q: What is the form of euthanasia called in which painkillers are given that may shorten life as a side effect?
74330.e: Here the aim is to relieve suffering; the possible shortening of life is only accepted. This form is considered permissible in Switzerland.
74330.m: In indirect active euthanasia, shortening of life is a side effect of pain relief.

74331.q: Which Swiss assisted dying organisation was founded in 1982?
74331.e: Exit (German-speaking Switzerland) was founded in 1982 and is the largest assisted dying organisation in Switzerland. It only accompanies members who live in Switzerland or have Swiss citizenship.
74331.m: Exit is the largest assisted dying organisation in Switzerland.

74332.q: Which lawyer founded the assisted dying organisation Dignitas in 1998?
74332.e: Ludwig A. Minelli founded Dignitas in Forch near Zurich. The organisation also accompanies people from abroad, which contributed internationally to the term ‘suicide tourism’.
74332.m: Dignitas was founded in 1998 by Ludwig A. Minelli.

74333.q: In a legal assisted suicide in Switzerland, what must the person wishing to die always do themselves?
a: Carry out the final act themselves
74333.e: In assisted suicide, the person capable of judgement must carry out the fatal act themselves. If another person carries it out, it counts as killing on request and is punishable.
74333.m: In assisted suicide, the person carries out the final act themselves.

74334.q: Which canton was the first, in 2012, to regulate assisted suicide in hospitals and care homes by popular vote?
74334.e: In June 2012, voters in Vaud accepted a counter-proposal requiring publicly subsidised homes and hospitals to allow assisted suicide under certain conditions. It was the first cantonal law of its kind.
74334.m: In 2012 Vaud was the first canton with a law on assisted suicide in institutions.

74335.q: In which canton was the controversial suicide capsule ‘Sarco’ used for the first time in September 2024?
74335.e: The capsule was used in a forest near Merishausen, after which the police arrested several people and opened criminal proceedings. The device had already been highly controversial legally.
74335.m: The first use of the Sarco capsule in Schaffhausen in 2024 led to criminal proceedings.

74336.q: How did Swiss voters decide on the factory farming initiative on 25 September 2022?
a: They rejected it with about 63 per cent
They accepted it with about 52 per cent
They rejected it with about 90 per cent
They accepted it with about 63 per cent
74336.e: The initiative wanted to anchor the dignity of farm animals in the constitution and require organic standards for all animal farming. Opponents pointed to Switzerland’s already strict animal welfare law.
74336.m: The factory farming initiative was clearly rejected in 2022.

74337.q: What is discrimination against living beings solely because of the species they belong to called?
74337.e: The term was coined by Richard Ryder in 1970, by analogy with racism and sexism. The criticism is that species alone is not a morally relevant feature.
74337.m: Speciesism is discrimination on the basis of species.

74338.q: Which philosopher wrote that the decisive question is not whether animals can think or speak, but whether they can suffer?
74338.e: Jeremy Bentham, a founder of utilitarianism, wrote the sentence ‘Can they suffer?’ in 1789. For him, the capacity to suffer was the reason for moral consideration.
74338.m: For Bentham, what counts with animals is the capacity to suffer.

74339.q: What do the three Rs that should be applied to animal experiments stand for?
74339.e: William Russell and Rex Burch formulated the 3R principle in 1959: replace animal experiments, reduce the number of animals and lessen the strain on them. In Switzerland, the 3R Competence Centre promotes these aims.
74339.m: Animal experiments should be replaced, reduced and refined.

74340.q: Which term has been in the Federal Constitution since 1992 and applies to animals, plants and other organisms?
74340.e: In 1992 Switzerland was one of the first countries to include the ‘dignity of living beings’ (Würde der Kreatur) in its constitution, today in Art. 120. The Animal Welfare Act explicitly protects the dignity of animals too.
74340.m: The Swiss constitution protects the dignity of living beings.

74341.q: Which ban did Switzerland’s first accepted popular initiative introduce in 1893?
74341.e: The initiative banned the slaughter of mammals without prior stunning. The ban still applies today in the Animal Welfare Act, although importing such meat is allowed.
74341.m: Switzerland’s first successful popular initiative required stunning before slaughter.

74342.q: Which philosopher founded a rights-based approach to animal ethics with ‘The Case for Animal Rights’ (1983)?
74342.e: Tom Regan sees animals as ‘subjects of a life’ with their own inherent value. For him this gives them rights that must not be traded off against benefits.
74342.m: Tom Regan grants animals rights as subjects of a life.

74343.q: Which 17th-century philosopher regarded animals as soulless automata?
74343.e: Descartes distinguished the thinking substance of humans from the mere mechanics of the body. For him, animals were machines without consciousness, which was later sharply criticised.
74343.m: Descartes considered animals to be machines without consciousness.

74344.q: What is the position in environmental ethics called according to which only humans have intrinsic moral value?
74344.e: In anthropocentrism (Greek anthropos, human), nature is worth protecting only because of its usefulness to humans. Even so, strong environmental duties can follow, for example towards future people.
74344.m: In anthropocentrism, humans are at the centre of morality.

74345.q: Which position grants intrinsic moral value to all living beings capable of suffering?
74345.e: Pathocentrism (Greek pathos, suffering) makes the capacity to feel the criterion. Many animals count, but not plants or ecosystems.
74345.m: For pathocentrism, whoever can suffer counts.

74346.q: Which doctor and theologian coined ‘reverence for life’ as the basis of a biocentric ethics?
74346.e: Albert Schweitzer developed the idea in Africa around 1915: all life wants to live and deserves respect. In 1953 he received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1952.
74346.m: Albert Schweitzer called for reverence for all life.

74347.q: Who formulated the ‘land ethic’, which gives moral consideration to ecosystems as a whole, in ‘A Sand County Almanac’ (1949)?
74347.e: Leopold wrote that an action is right when it preserves the integrity, stability and beauty of the biotic community. His land ethic is a classic of ecocentrism.
74347.m: Aldo Leopold’s land ethic looks at whole ecosystems.

74348.q: Which Norwegian philosopher coined the term ‘deep ecology’ in 1973?
74348.e: Arne Naess distinguished a ‘shallow’ ecology, which protects the environment only for humans, from a ‘deep’ one, which grants all life intrinsic value. Deep ecology influenced many environmental movements.
74348.m: Arne Naess’s deep ecology grants all life intrinsic value.

74349.q: Who first applied the idea of sustainability to forestry in 1713?
74349.e: In his ‘Sylvicultura oeconomica’, the Saxon mining official demanded that only as much wood be cut as grows back. The term later became a guiding principle of environmental policy.
74349.m: Sustainability originally means not cutting more wood than grows back.

74350.q: According to which principle should those who cause environmental damage bear its costs?
74350.e: The polluter pays principle is anchored in the Swiss Environmental Protection Act and in Art. 74 of the Federal Constitution. One example is waste charges such as the fee on rubbish bags.
74350.m: Whoever pollutes the environment should pay for it.

74351.q: Which principle requires possible environmental damage to be prevented even when there is still scientific uncertainty?
74351.e: The precautionary principle was set down, for example, in the 1992 Rio Declaration. A lack of full certainty should not be a reason to postpone protective measures.
74351.m: When environmental damage threatens, you should not wait for complete certainty.

74352.q: Which economist wrote in 1970 that the social responsibility of a business is to increase its profits?
74352.e: In the ‘New York Times’, Milton Friedman argued that managers are obliged to the owners as long as they keep to the rules of the game. The thesis is often quoted as the opposite of corporate responsibility.
74352.m: Friedman saw increasing profits as the only social duty of businesses.

74353.q: What is the approach called according to which companies should take into account the interests of all stakeholder groups such as staff, customers and the environment?
74353.e: R. Edward Freeman made the stakeholder approach well known in 1984. It contrasts with focusing purely on the shareholders.
74353.m: The stakeholder approach takes all of a company’s stakeholder groups seriously.

74354.q: Which work did Adam Smith publish in 1759, years before his ‘Wealth of Nations’?
74354.e: In ‘The Theory of Moral Sentiments’, Smith explains morality through sympathy and the view of an ‘impartial spectator’. Smith saw himself as a moral philosopher, not only as an economist.
74354.m: Adam Smith was a moral philosopher before he became a classic of economics.

74355.q: Why did the Responsible Business Initiative fail on 29 November 2020?
a: It did not win a majority of the cantons
It did not win a majority of the people
The Federal Supreme Court stopped it
74355.e: The initiative received about 50.7 per cent yes votes, but a majority of the cantons rejected it. Instead, the indirect counter-proposal with reporting obligations came into force.
74355.m: A popular initiative needs a majority of both the people and the cantons.

74356.q: In which country was the first Fairtrade label ‘Max Havelaar’ created in 1988?
74356.e: The label was named after the main character of a Dutch novel that criticises exploitation on coffee plantations. The Swiss Max Havelaar Foundation followed in 1992.
74356.m: The Fairtrade label Max Havelaar comes from the Netherlands.

74357.q: At which university did Peter Ulrich develop integrative business ethics?
74357.e: From 1987 Peter Ulrich held the first chair of business ethics in the German-speaking world. His integrative business ethics asks what kind of good life the economy should serve.
74357.m: Integrative business ethics comes from St Gallen.

74358.q: Which UN initiative of 2000 invites companies to respect ten principles on human rights, labour, the environment and fighting corruption?
74358.e: The Global Compact goes back to a speech by UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan in Davos in 1999. Taking part is voluntary, and companies report on their progress every year.
74358.m: In the UN Global Compact, companies voluntarily commit to ten principles.

74359.q: What is it called when a company presents itself in advertising as more environmentally friendly than it really is?
74359.e: Greenwashing is made up of ‘green’ and ‘whitewashing’ (glossing over). It deceives consumers and undermines real sustainability.

74360.q: According to which basic approach does the EU’s 2024 AI Act classify AI systems?
74360.e: The AI Act distinguishes unacceptable, high, limited and minimal risk. The higher the risk, the stricter the obligations.
74360.m: The EU AI Act regulates AI according to its risk.

74361.q: Which AI application does the EU AI Act ban as an unacceptable risk?
74361.e: In social scoring, people are given a score based on their behaviour, which can lead to disadvantages. The EU sees this as a violation of human dignity and equal treatment.
74361.m: Social scoring is banned in the EU.

74362.q: What are systematic distortions called through which an AI system disadvantages certain groups?
74362.e: Bias often arises because training data contain existing prejudices. Facial recognition systems, for example, have been shown to recognise people with dark skin less well.
74362.m: Biased data lead to biased AI decisions.

74363.q: What is the research field called that aims to make the decisions of AI systems understandable to people?
74363.e: Many learning systems are regarded as a ‘black box’ because the way they reach a decision is unclear. Explainable AI (XAI) is meant to make transparency and control possible.
74363.m: Explainable AI makes the reasons for a machine’s decision visible.

74364.q: Which writer formulated the three laws of robotics in 1942?
74364.e: The laws appeared in the short story ‘Runaround’. The first forbids a robot to injure a human; they are still quoted in AI debates today.
74364.m: Asimov’s laws of robotics are an early attempt to give machines a morality.

74365.q: Which organisation adopted the first legally binding international treaty on AI and human rights in 2024?
74365.e: The Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence and Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law is also open to states outside Europe. Switzerland helped to draft it.
74365.m: In 2024 the Council of Europe created the first binding international treaty on AI.

74366.q: What are deceptively real-looking fakes of videos, images or voices created with AI called?
74366.e: The term is made up of ‘deep learning’ and ‘fake’. Deepfakes are ethically problematic, for example, in disinformation, fraud or damaging someone’s reputation.
74366.m: Deepfakes are AI fakes that look real.

74367.q: What is the challenge called of designing AI systems so that their goals match human values?
74367.e: The alignment problem asks how to make sure that an AI does what people really want. Even small errors in setting the goal can lead to unwanted behaviour.
74367.m: Alignment is about tying AI to human values.

74368.q: Since when has the revised Swiss Federal Act on Data Protection been in force?
74368.e: The fully revised Data Protection Act brought Swiss law into line with digital developments and European standards. It now protects only data of natural persons.
74368.m: The new Swiss Data Protection Act has applied since September 2023.

74369.q: Which authority in Switzerland supervises compliance with data protection by federal bodies and private parties?
74369.e: The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner (FDPIC) can open investigations and, since 2023, issue binding orders. The cantons have their own data protection officers for cantonal bodies.
74369.m: The FDPIC watches over data protection in Switzerland.

74370.q: Since which date has the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) applied?
74370.e: The GDPR was adopted in 2016 and has applied since 25 May 2018. It also applies to Swiss companies that offer goods or services to people in the EU.
74370.m: The GDPR has applied since May 2018.

74371.q: What does the right to informational self-determination mean?
a: Each person basically decides for themselves about the disclosure and use of their data
The state decides what information you may read
Each person may freely use all data of others
Companies may sell data without consent
74371.e: The right was formulated in 1983 by the German Federal Constitutional Court in its census ruling. It also shapes Swiss and European data protection law.
74371.m: Informational self-determination means: I decide about my data.

74372.q: What is the principle called of processing only as much personal data as is needed for the purpose?
74372.e: Data minimisation is one of the basic principles of the GDPR and in Swiss law is part of proportionality. What is not collected cannot be misused.
74372.m: You should only collect the data you really need.

74373.q: What is the principle called of building data protection into a system technically right from its development?
74373.e: The concept was coined by the Canadian privacy commissioner Ann Cavoukian. The revised Swiss Data Protection Act explicitly requires data protection by design and privacy-friendly default settings.
74373.m: Data protection should be built into technology from the start.

74374.q: Which company used data from millions of Facebook profiles without consent for political advertising, as became known in 2018?
74374.e: Data from up to 87 million profiles were harvested through a quiz app. The scandal sparked worldwide debates about data power and election manipulation.
74374.m: The Cambridge Analytica scandal showed the political power of personal data.

74375.q: Which right did the European Court of Justice recognise in 2014 in the ‘Google Spain’ case?
74375.e: Under certain circumstances, search engines must remove links to outdated or inappropriate information about a person. This is weighed against the public interest in information.
74375.m: The right to be forgotten protects against old information being findable for ever.

74376.q: In which year did the Federal Council set up the National Advisory Commission on Biomedical Ethics (NEK)?
74376.e: The Federal Council set up the NEK on 3 July 2001. It advises politicians and the public on ethical questions in medicine and health care.

74377.q: Which area is the National Ethics Commission NEK responsible for in Switzerland?
74377.e: Its full German name means ‘National Ethics Commission in the Field of Human Medicine’, abbreviated CNE in French. It deals, for example, with questions at the end of life, vaccinations or organ donation.
74377.m: The NEK deals with ethical questions in human medicine.

74378.q: At which federal office is the NEK’s secretariat based?
74378.e: Administratively, the NEK is attached to the Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) in Bern. In terms of content, it works independently and is not bound by instructions.
74378.m: The NEK is based at the FOPH but works independently.

74379.q: Who in Switzerland carries out the ethical review of individual research projects on humans, which the NEK explicitly does not do?
74379.e: Under the Human Research Act, cantonal ethics committees approve specific research projects. The NEK, by contrast, comments on fundamental questions and not on individual applications.
74379.m: Cantonal ethics committees review specific research projects.

74380.q: Which system for organ donation did the NEK recommend in 2019 instead of the opt-out system?
74380.e: In the declaration system, people are regularly asked to state their views on organ donation. The NEK considered the opt-out system ethically problematic because silence should not count as consent.
74380.m: In 2019 the NEK wanted people to state their views on organ donation explicitly.

74381.q: Which commission has dealt with ethical questions of biotechnology and genetic engineering in animals, plants and other organisms in Switzerland since 1998?
74381.e: The Federal Ethics Committee on Non-Human Biotechnology (ECNH) was set up by the Federal Council in 1998. It has dealt, for example, with the dignity of plants.
74381.m: The ECNH is responsible for biotechnology outside humans.

74382.q: What kind of body is the NEK?
74382.e: Extra-parliamentary commissions are expert bodies of the Confederation whose members are elected by the Federal Council. They contribute expertise without passing laws themselves.
74382.m: The NEK is an extra-parliamentary commission elected by the Federal Council.

74383.q: Which task is part of the NEK’s legal mandate?
74383.e: The NEK writes opinions, advises authorities on request and informs the public. In this way society should be able to discuss ethical questions in medicine widely.
74383.m: The NEK advises and promotes public debate on ethics.

74384.q: Which UN report of 1987 defined sustainable development as taking into account the needs of future generations?
a: Report to the Club of Rome
74384.e: The report ‘Our Common Future’, led by the Norwegian Gro Harlem Brundtland, gave the best-known definition: meeting the needs of the present without taking away the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
74384.m: Sustainable means leaving future generations their chances.

74385.q: What is the unspoken agreement called that the younger generation finances the pensions of the older one?
74385.e: The generational contract is not a real contract but an image for solidarity between age groups. It assumes that today’s contributors will also be provided for later.
74385.m: The generational contract links young and old in pension provision.

74386.q: Which instrument, accepted by the people in 2001, is meant to stop the Confederation permanently passing debts on to future generations?
74386.e: The debt brake was accepted with about 85 per cent yes and has been applied since 2003. Over an economic cycle, spending should not exceed revenue.
74386.m: The debt brake keeps federal finances in balance over time.

74387.q: Which association won a ruling of the European Court of Human Rights against Switzerland on 9 April 2024 for insufficient climate protection?
a: KlimaSeniorinnen Schweiz (Senior Women for Climate Protection)
74387.e: The ECtHR found that Switzerland had violated the right to respect for private and family life because it was doing too little against climate change. The ruling is often discussed in connection with duties towards those affected and coming generations.
74387.m: The KlimaSeniorinnen won against Switzerland in Strasbourg in 2024.

74388.q: What is the procedure called of giving future costs and benefits less weight in calculations than present ones?
74388.e: The higher the discount rate, the less future climate damage counts today. That is why choosing the rate is an ethical question of justice between generations.
74388.m: Discounting makes future damage smaller in today’s calculations.

74389.q: Which popular initiative did Swiss voters accept on 3 March 2024?
a: Initiative for a 13th AHV pension payment
74389.e: The initiative was accepted with about 58 per cent, while the pensions initiative to raise the retirement age was clearly rejected on the same day. The debate focused strongly on sharing the burden between young and old.
74389.m: In 2024 the voters decided on a 13th AHV pension payment.

74390.q: Which country created the office of a commissioner for future generations by law in 2015?
74390.e: The ‘Well-being of Future Generations (Wales) Act’ requires public bodies to consider the long-term consequences of their decisions. A commissioner monitors this.
74390.m: Wales has its own commissioner for future generations.

74391.q: Which former employee of an NSA contractor made the worldwide mass surveillance by US intelligence services public in 2013?
74391.e: Edward Snowden handed journalists secret documents about programmes such as PRISM. He fled via Hong Kong to Russia and has lived there ever since.
74391.m: Snowden revealed the NSA’s mass surveillance in 2013.

74392.q: Which military analyst gave the ‘Pentagon Papers’ on the Vietnam War to the press in 1971?
74392.e: The secret study showed that several US governments had misled the public about the war. The Supreme Court allowed the press to publish it.
74392.m: In 1971 Ellsberg made the deception about the Vietnam War public.

74393.q: Which security guard in Zurich in January 1997 saved bank files from being shredded that were connected with dormant assets from the Nazi era?
74393.e: Christoph Meili worked as a night watchman at the Union Bank of Switzerland. After threats he was granted asylum in the USA, but later returned to Switzerland.
74393.m: In 1997 Christoph Meili became Switzerland’s best-known whistleblower.

74394.q: Which computer specialist took customer data from the HSBC private bank in Geneva and handed it to tax authorities?
74394.e: The data were later analysed internationally as ‘Swiss Leaks’. In 2015 the Federal Criminal Court convicted Falciani in his absence of economic espionage.
74394.m: Hervé Falciani’s data led to the Swiss Leaks.

74395.q: When did the EU adopt a directive to protect people who report breaches of EU law?
74395.e: The Whistleblower Directive requires secure reporting channels and forbids retaliation such as dismissal. Member states had to implement it by the end of 2021.
74395.m: Since 2019 the EU has protected whistleblowers with its own directive.

74396.q: What happened in 2020 in the National Council to the bill to protect whistleblowers in the private sector?
a: It went to a popular vote
It was handed over to the cantons
74396.e: The National Council sank the revision of the Code of Obligations after more than ten years of debate. For critics it did not go far enough, for others it went too far.
74396.m: In 2020 special protection for whistleblowers in the private sector failed in the National Council.

74397.q: To which body can employees of the federal administration report wrongdoing?
74397.e: Since 2011 the Federal Personnel Act has provided for a reporting office at the Swiss Federal Audit Office (SFAO). Anyone who reports in good faith must not be put at a disadvantage because of it.
74397.m: Federal employees can report wrongdoing to the Federal Audit Office.

74398.q: Under which code name did FBI deputy director Mark Felt help journalists uncover the Watergate affair?
74398.e: Mark Felt only revealed himself in 2005 as the source of Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein. The affair led to the resignation of President Richard Nixon in 1974.
74398.m: Deep Throat was the secret source in the Watergate scandal.

74399.q: What characterises a genuine moral dilemma?
74399.e: In a dilemma, you can fulfil only one of two well-founded duties and so inevitably violate the other. There is no way out without moral loss.
74399.m: In a dilemma, every choice violates a duty.

74400.q: Which psychologist used the Heinz dilemma to study the stages of moral development?
74400.e: In the Heinz dilemma, a man considers whether to steal an unaffordable medicine for his dying wife. Kohlberg was mainly interested in the reasoning behind the answer, not in the answer itself.
74400.m: Kohlberg assessed the reasoning in the Heinz dilemma.

74401.q: What is the highest level of moral development according to Lawrence Kohlberg called?
74401.e: At this level, people are guided by universal principles such as justice, even against existing rules. Kohlberg assumed that only a few adults reach it.
74401.m: Postconventional morality follows general principles rather than mere rules.

74402.q: What is the ancient thought experiment called in which two shipwrecked people fight over a plank that can carry only one?
74402.e: The Greek philosopher Carneades asked whether you may push the other person away to save yourself. In law, this is an example of an excusing necessity.
74402.m: The plank of Carneades asks whether you may save yourself at another’s expense.

74403.q: What is the problem described in the journal ‘Science’ in 1968 called, that freely accessible common goods are overused?
74403.e: When each person takes their own advantage from a shared pasture, it is destroyed for everyone. The economist Elinor Ostrom later showed that communities such as Swiss alpine pasture cooperatives can prevent this.
74403.m: Without rules, common goods risk being overused.

74404.q: What is the situation called in which two people questioned separately both end up worse off through selfish action than if they had cooperated?
74404.e: For each person individually, betrayal pays, but together keeping silent would be better. This model from game theory shows why trust and rules are important for cooperation.
74404.m: In the prisoner’s dilemma, self-interest leads both to a worse result.

74406.q: Which principle, going back to Thomas Aquinas, allows a good action under certain conditions despite a foreseeable bad side effect?
74406.e: The bad consequence must not be intended and must not be the means to the end, and there must be an appropriate reason. The principle is often applied in medical ethics and the ethics of war.
74406.m: Under the principle of double effect, what counts is what you intend and what you merely accept.

74407.q: What did the ecologist Garrett Hardin argue with his ‘lifeboat ethics’?
a: Aid from rich countries to poor ones should be limited
All people should share goods equally
Rich countries should take in unlimited refugees
Aid should only go through the churches
74407.e: Hardin compared rich countries to a lifeboat that sinks when overcrowded, and therefore rejected unlimited aid. His position was strongly criticised for its harshness.
74407.m: Lifeboat ethics asks whether aid may have limits.

74408.q: Which part of the computer do you use to type letters?
74408.e: On the keyboard there is a key for every letter. When you press it, the letter appears on the screen.
74408.m: You write letters and numbers with the keyboard.

74409.q: Where do you see the computer's pictures and texts?
74409.e: The screen shows everything the computer does. It is also called a monitor.
74409.m: The screen shows pictures and texts.

74410.q: What do you use to move the pointer on the screen?
74410.e: When you slide the mouse back and forth on the table, the pointer moves with it. With a click you choose something.
74410.m: You move the pointer with the mouse.

74411.q: Which device puts a text from the computer onto paper?
74411.e: The printer prints texts and pictures onto paper. That way you can hold them in your hand.
74411.m: The printer puts texts onto paper.

74412.q: Which part plays sounds and music?
74412.e: Sounds, voices and music come out of the loudspeaker. You can also plug in headphones.
74412.m: Sounds come out of the loudspeaker.

74413.q: Which part lets the computer record your voice?
74413.e: The microphone records sounds, for example your voice. That way you can talk to others or record a song.
74413.m: The microphone records sounds and voices.

74414.q: What is the part called that calculates and thinks inside the computer?
74414.e: The processor is a small chip in the computer. It carries out all the commands and calculates very fast.
74414.m: The processor is the computer's brain.

74415.q: What does a computer need to work at all?
74415.e: A computer only works with electricity. It gets it from the socket or from a battery.

74416.q: What is a computer called that you can fold shut and take with you?
74416.e: In a laptop, the screen, keyboard and battery are in one device. You can fold it shut and take it anywhere.
74416.m: You can fold a laptop shut and take it with you.

74417.q: Which set of instructions from everyday life is similar to an algorithm?
74417.e: A recipe says exactly which steps you have to do one after the other. An algorithm works in exactly the same way.
74417.m: A recipe is like an algorithm.

74418.q: What must the steps in an algorithm be like?
74418.e: A computer does not understand vague instructions. That is why every step must be clear and unambiguous.
74418.m: Every step in an algorithm must be clear.

74419.q: What do building instructions for blocks tell you?
74419.e: Building instructions show step by step which piece goes where. That is why they are like an algorithm.
74419.m: Building instructions show step by step how to build something.

74420.q: What happens if a step is missing from a set of instructions?
74420.e: If a step is missing, you do not know what to do. The result is then often wrong.
74420.m: Good instructions have no missing steps.

74421.q: What is the first step when brushing your teeth?
74421.e: First the toothpaste goes on the toothbrush. Only then can you brush your teeth.
74421.m: Brushing your teeth also has a fixed order.

74422.q: What does a computer do with an algorithm?
74422.e: The computer works through the steps of the algorithm exactly in order. It only does what is written there.
74422.m: A computer carries out algorithms step by step.

74423.q: An algorithm says: “Take 2 steps, then 3 more steps.” How many steps is that?
74423.e: You work out 2 + 3 = 5. So you take 5 steps in total.
74423.m: You can add up the steps of a set of instructions.

74424.q: What is a command for a computer?
74424.e: A command tells the computer what to do. Many commands one after the other make a program.
74424.m: A command tells the computer what to do.

74425.q: What do you call many commands for a computer one after the other?
74425.e: A program is made of many commands in a fixed order. The computer works through them one after the other.
74425.m: A program is made of many commands.

74426.q: What is the right order when getting dressed?
74426.e: The socks have to go on your feet first. Only then do the shoes fit over them.
74426.m: The order of commands is important.

74427.q: What happens if you swap commands around?
74427.e: The computer does exactly what is in the order given. If commands are swapped, something different often comes out.
74427.m: Swapped commands can lead to a wrong result.

74428.q: What do you call a mistake in a program?
74428.e: A bug is really a small insect. That is what people call a mistake in a program.
74428.m: A mistake in a program is called a bug.

74429.q: What do you call looking for mistakes in a program and fixing them?
74429.e: When debugging, you look for the bugs, meaning the mistakes, and correct them. After that the program works properly.
74429.m: When debugging, you find and fix mistakes.

74430.q: What is a loop in a program?
74430.e: In a loop, a command is repeated several times. That way you do not have to write it again each time.
74430.m: A loop repeats commands several times.

74431.q: A command “Clap!” is repeated 3 times. How many times do you clap?
74431.e: The command is carried out 3 times. That is why you clap 3 times.
74431.m: A repetition carries out the same command several times.

74432.q: What is the name of a well-known programming language with colourful blocks for children?
74432.e: In Scratch you put colourful command blocks together like jigsaw pieces. You can use it to program games and stories.
74432.m: In Scratch you program with colourful blocks.

74433.q: What does an educational robot do?
74433.e: You give an educational robot commands. It carries them out exactly as you entered them.
74433.m: An educational robot carries out the commands you give it.

74434.q: An educational robot is facing forwards. What does it do with the command “forwards”?
74434.e: With “forwards”, the robot moves one step in the direction it is facing.
74434.m: With the command forwards, the robot moves forwards.

74435.q: A robot is facing north and makes a quarter turn to the right. Which way is it facing now?
74435.e: If you turn a quarter turn to the right from north, you face east. To the left it would be west.
74435.m: To the right of north is east.

74436.q: A robot makes a quarter turn to the left twice. Which way is it facing then?
74436.e: Two quarter turns make a half turn. The robot then faces exactly the other way.
74436.m: Two quarter turns make a half turn.

74437.q: A robot moves 3 squares forwards and then 1 square backwards. How many squares is it from the start?
74437.e: It moves 3 forwards and 1 back. 3 minus 1 makes 2 squares.
74437.m: Moving backwards brings the robot closer to the start again.

74438.q: How does a small educational robot like Blue-Bot get its commands?
74438.e: With the Blue-Bot, you press arrow buttons on its back or use a tablet. Then you press Go.
74438.m: You give an educational robot commands with buttons.

74439.q: How far does the Blue-Bot move with one step forwards?
74439.e: The Blue-Bot and the Bee-Bot move about 15 centimetres per step. That is why there are matching play mats with squares.
74439.m: The Blue-Bot moves about 15 centimetres per step.

74440.q: Where does an educational robot get its energy from?
74440.e: Educational robots have a rechargeable battery or normal batteries. You charge the rechargeable battery with electricity again.
74440.m: An educational robot needs a rechargeable battery or batteries.

74441.m: In this sequence you always add 2.

74442.q: How does the pattern continue: circle, circle, star, circle, circle, ...?
74442.e: The pattern is always two circles, then one star. After two circles comes the star.
74442.m: In a pattern, a group repeats again and again.

74443.q: Secret code: A=1, B=2, C=3. Which word is 2 1?
74443.e: 2 stands for B and 1 stands for A. Together that makes BA.
74443.m: In a code, one sign stands for another.

74444.q: Which two digits does a computer calculate with inside?
74444.e: Inside, the computer only knows two states, on and off. They are written as 1 and 0.
74444.m: Inside, a computer calculates with 0 and 1.

74445.e: A QR code is a square made of black and white dots. A mobile phone can read it and, for example, open a website.
74445.m: A QR code is a picture code a mobile phone can read.

74446.q: Where do you find a barcode in a shop?
74446.e: There is a barcode on almost every packet. The till reads it and so knows the price.
74446.m: The till reads the barcode on the packaging.

74447.q: In Morse code there are dots and ...?
74447.e: Morse code is made up of short and long signals. They are written as dots and dashes.
74447.m: Morse code is made up of dots and dashes.

74448.q: How many answers are there to a yes-no question?
74448.e: You answer a yes-no question only with yes or no. Those are two possibilities.
74448.m: A yes-no question has two possible answers.

74449.q: Which question is a yes-no question?
74449.e: To “Do you have a dog?” you can only say yes or no. The other questions need a longer answer.
74449.m: You can answer a yes-no question with yes or no.

74450.e: An apple is a fruit. It grows on a tree and is not an animal.
74450.m: An apple is a fruit and not an animal.

74451.q: What do you call a plan that leads to a solution with yes-no questions?
74451.e: In a decision tree, you go one way for yes and the other way for no. In the end you reach the solution.
74451.m: A decision tree leads to the solution with yes-no questions.

74452.q: You are looking for a number from 1 to 4. After how many clever yes-no questions do you know it for sure?
74452.e: First ask: “Is it bigger than 2?” Then only 2 numbers are left, and a second question is enough.
74452.m: With clever questions you find the solution faster.

74453.q: What is a good first question for guessing an animal?
74453.e: The question “Can it fly?” divides many animals into two groups. That way lots of animals are ruled out at once.
74453.m: A good question divides the possibilities into two groups.

74454.q: If it rains, you take an umbrella. It is raining. What do you do?
74454.e: The answer to “Is it raining?” is yes. So the rule applies, and you take the umbrella with you.
74454.m: With yes you follow the rule, with no you do not.

74455.q: A small light has two states. Which ones?
74455.e: A small light is either on or off. That is like yes or no for a computer.
74455.m: On and off is like yes and no.

74456.q: Which numbers are sorted by size?
74456.e: In 1, 3, 5, 7 each number gets bigger. The smallest number is at the front.
74456.m: When sorting, the smallest number comes first.

74457.q: Which word comes first in alphabetical order?
74457.e: Apple begins with A. A is right at the front of the alphabet.
74457.m: In the alphabet, A is right at the front.

74458.q: You sort 9, 2, 6. Which number is then in the middle?
74458.e: Sorted, it reads 2, 6, 9. The 6 is in the middle.
74458.m: Sorted numbers are in order of size.

74459.q: Children line up by height. Who is right at the front?
74459.e: If you sort from small to tall, the smallest child is at the front. The tallest is at the back.
74459.m: From small to tall, the smallest is at the front.

74460.q: Which word comes last in alphabetical order?
74460.e: Zebra begins with Z. Z is the last letter of the alphabet.
74460.m: Z is the last letter of the alphabet.

74461.e: You find something much faster in a sorted list. That is why dictionaries are in alphabetical order.

74462.q: How are the words in a dictionary sorted?
74462.e: In a dictionary, all the words are in alphabetical order. That way you can find any word quickly.
74462.m: In a dictionary, the words are in alphabetical order.

74463.q: Which number is the biggest in 8, 3, 11, 5?
74463.e: 11 is more than 8, 5 and 3. That is why 11 is the biggest number.
74463.m: When sorting, you always compare two things.

74464.q: What do you need a password for?
74464.e: A password protects your account or device. Only someone who knows the password can get in.

74465.e: Lots of people use 1234. That is why thieves try this sequence of numbers first.
74465.m: Simple sequences of numbers are bad passwords.

74466.q: What is better as a password?
74466.e: A long, made-up sentence is hard to guess. Other people often know names and birthdays too.
74466.m: A long sentence is a good password.

74467.q: What is a short number password for a mobile phone called?
74467.e: The PIN is a secret number, often with 4 or 6 digits. You use it to unlock your phone, for example.
74467.m: The PIN is a secret number.

74468.q: What do you do if someone knows your password who should not?
74468.e: You should change the password at once. It is best to get help from an adult when you do.
74468.m: If a password has been given away, change it at once.

74469.q: Where should you not write down a password?
a: On a note stuck to the screen
In a notebook kept by your parents
74469.e: Anyone can read a note on the screen. Then the password is no longer secret.
74469.m: A password should not be visible on the screen.

74470.q: What is a network without cables that lets you get onto the internet called?
74470.e: With Wi-Fi, a device connects to the internet by radio. You do not need a cable for it.
74470.m: With Wi-Fi you get onto the internet without a cable.

74471.q: What do you call a page on the internet?
74471.e: A web page has texts, pictures or games on it. You open it with a browser.
74471.m: A page on the internet is called a web page.

74472.q: What do you use to find something on the internet?
74472.e: You type a word into a search engine. It then shows matching web pages.
74472.m: A search engine helps you search the internet.

74473.q: What do you do if something on the internet frightens you?
a: Look at it for a long time
74473.e: Tell your parents or your teacher. They can help you.
74473.m: If something on the internet frightens me, I tell an adult.

74474.q: What do you not tell strangers on the internet?
74474.e: Your address is private. Strangers on the internet should not know where you live.
74474.m: I do not give my address away on the internet.

74475.q: What do you do so that a drawing on the computer does not get lost?
74475.e: When you save, the computer stores your work. That way you can open it again later.
74475.m: What you save, you can open again later.

74476.q: What do you call a saved picture or text on the computer?
74476.e: Every piece of saved work is a file. It has a name so that you can find it again.
74476.m: A saved text or picture is a file.

74477.q: What can you organise files on the computer in?
74477.e: On the computer there are folders, like in an office. You put files that belong together into a folder.
74477.m: You can organise files in folders.

74478.q: What happens if you forget to save and the power goes off?
74478.e: Anything that has not been saved can be lost in a power cut. That is why you save often.
74478.m: If you save often, you lose less work.

74479.q: Where does a deleted file often go first?
74479.e: Many computers put deleted files into the recycle bin first. From there you can still get them back.
74479.m: You can often get files back from the recycle bin.

74480.e: You can save files onto a USB stick. It is small and fits in your trouser pocket.
74480.m: You can carry files around on a USB stick.

74481.q: What is storage space on the internet called?
74481.e: In the cloud, files are kept on computers on the internet, far away like a cloud in the sky.
74481.m: In the cloud you save files on the internet.

74482.q: What does every file need so that you can find it again?
74482.e: Every file gets a name when it is saved. A good name helps when searching.
74482.m: A good file name helps you find it again.

74483.q: What do you usually use to operate a tablet?
74483.e: A tablet has a touchscreen. You tap and swipe on it with your fingers.
74483.m: You operate a tablet with your fingers.

74484.q: What is a screen called that you operate with your finger?
74484.e: A touchscreen is a screen that reacts to touch. It notices where you tap it.
74484.m: You operate a touchscreen by touching it.

74485.q: What do you call a program on a tablet?
74485.e: App is short for application. There are apps for learning, painting or playing.
74485.m: A program on a tablet is called an app.

74486.q: What do you have to do regularly with a tablet's battery?
74486.e: The battery stores electricity. When it is empty, you have to connect the tablet to the charger.
74486.m: You have to charge a tablet's battery.

74487.q: What does a tablet usually not have?
74487.e: On a tablet, the keyboard appears on the screen. A fixed keyboard like a laptop's is usually missing.
74487.m: On a tablet, the keyboard appears on the screen.

74488.q: What can you use to take photos with a tablet?
74488.e: Most tablets have a camera on the front and back. You use it to take photos and videos.
74488.m: You take photos with the tablet's camera.

74489.q: Why should you not look at a tablet for too long?
74489.e: Looking at a screen for a long time tires your eyes. Breaks and moving about do you good.
74489.m: After screen time you need breaks.

74490.q: What do you do with two fingers to make a picture bigger on a tablet?
74490.e: If you spread two fingers apart on the screen, the picture gets bigger. Pinching them together makes it smaller.
74490.m: You can make a picture bigger with two fingers.

74491.q: What is a picture on the screen made of?
74491.e: Lots of small pixels next to each other make a picture together. From a distance you cannot see the individual dots.
74491.m: A screen picture is made of lots of pixels.

74492.q: What colour does a pixel show when it does not light up at all?
74492.e: Without light, a pixel looks dark. That is why a screen that is switched off looks black.
74492.m: A pixel without light looks black.

74493.q: What do you see if you enlarge a picture a great deal?
74493.e: Greatly enlarged, you see the individual pixels. They look like small squares.
74493.m: Greatly enlarged, you see the pixels as small squares.

74494.q: A pixel picture has 3 rows with 4 pixels each. How many pixels is that?
74494.m: You count pixels as rows times columns.

74495.q: When does a picture look sharper?
74495.e: With more and smaller pixels you see more details. The picture then looks sharper.
74495.m: More pixels make a picture sharper.

74496.q: What is art made of a few clearly visible pixels called?
74496.e: In pixel art you paint with individual squares. Old video games often looked like this.
74496.m: Pixel art is art made of individual pixels.

74497.q: From which three colours of light does a screen mix all colours?
74497.e: Every pixel has tiny lights in red, green and blue. Mixed together they make all the colours.
74497.m: A screen mixes colours from red, green and blue.

74498.q: You sort 4, 1, 3, 2 from biggest to smallest. Which number is at the front?
74498.e: From biggest to smallest means 4, 3, 2, 1. The biggest number, 4, is at the front.
74498.m: From biggest to smallest, the biggest number is at the front.

74499.q: A robot should move 4 squares forwards. How many times do you press the forwards button?
74499.e: Each press of the button is one square. For 4 squares you press it 4 times.
74499.m: The robot needs one command for each square.

74500.q: Who was the programming language Scratch mainly developed for?
a: For children and young people learning to program
74500.e: Scratch was developed at MIT in the USA and released in 2007. Its colourful blocks are meant to help children and young people in particular learn to program easily.
74500.m: Scratch was developed for children and young people.

74501.q: How do you build a program in Scratch?
74501.e: Scratch is a block-based language: the commands are colourful blocks that you fit together like jigsaw pieces.
74501.m: In Scratch you fit command blocks together like jigsaw pieces.

74502.q: In Scratch, what are the objects you program, for example the cat, called?
74502.e: In Scratch, the programmable objects are called sprites. Each sprite has its own scripts.

74503.q: In Scratch, what is the area on which the sprites move called?
74503.e: The sprites appear and move on the stage. The stage itself can also have scripts and different backdrops.
74503.m: In Scratch, the sprites perform on the stage.

74504.q: What are the coordinates of the centre of the stage in Scratch?
74504.e: The stage is set up like a coordinate system whose origin (0, 0) is exactly in the centre.
74504.m: In Scratch, the centre of the stage has the coordinates zero and zero.

74505.q: Between which x values does the stage lie in Scratch?
74505.e: The stage is 480 points wide and 360 points high. That is why x goes from -240 to 240 and y from -180 to 180.
74505.m: The Scratch stage is 480 points wide and 360 points high.

74506.q: What do you use several costumes for a sprite for in Scratch?
74506.e: If a sprite switches quickly between slightly different costumes, it looks as though it is moving, for example walking.
74506.m: With changing costumes you can animate a sprite.

74507.q: Which animal is Scratch's well-known mascot?
74507.e: The orange Scratch cat is the default sprite that is already on the stage in every new project.

74508.q: A sprite is at x = 0 and facing right. It carries out “move 10 steps” three times. Where is it afterwards?
74508.e: Each command moves the sprite 10 steps to the right: 0 + 10 + 10 + 10 makes 30.
74508.m: Every step to the right increases the x value.

74509.q: In Python, how many times is the indented command under “for i in range(5):” carried out?
74509.e: range(5) gives the numbers 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4. That is 5 values, so the loop runs five times.
74509.m: The loop with range(5) runs exactly five times.

74510.q: A sprite carries out: “repeat 4: move 100 steps, turn 90 degrees”. Which shape does it draw?
74510.e: Four sides of equal length, each followed by a turn of 90 degrees, make a square, because 4 times 90 degrees is 360 degrees.
74510.m: Four sides with right angles make a square.

74511.q: A sprite should draw an equilateral triangle using “repeat 3”. By how many degrees must it turn after each side?
74511.e: Going all the way round, the sprite turns 360 degrees in total. With three corners that is 360 ÷ 3, so 120 degrees per corner.
74511.m: The turns of a closed shape add up to 360 degrees.

74512.q: A “repeat 3” loop is inside a “repeat 4” loop. Inside it is “play sound Meow”. How many times does the sprite meow?
74512.e: With nested loops, the inner loop runs all the way through on each pass of the outer loop: 4 times 3 makes 12.
74512.m: With nested loops, you multiply the numbers of repetitions.

74513.q: A program: “set x to 0”, then “repeat 5: change x by 3”. What value does x have at the end?
74513.e: x starts at 0 and is increased by 3 five times: 0 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 makes 15.
74513.m: A loop can increase a value step by step.

74514.q: When does the Scratch block “repeat until” stop?
a: Never, it keeps going for ever
74514.e: “Repeat until” carries out the commands until the given condition is met, meaning it is true.
74514.m: “Repeat until” runs until the condition is met.

74515.q: Which loop do you use when the number of repetitions is fixed in advance?
74515.e: A counting loop repeats the commands a fixed number of times, for example “repeat 10” in Scratch or “for” in Python.
74515.m: A counting loop repeats commands a fixed number of times.

74516.q: What do you call a loop that never ends by itself?
74516.e: An infinite loop keeps running without end. In Scratch you create one on purpose with “forever”, for example for games.
74516.m: An infinite loop never stops by itself.

74517.q: Which Scratch block carries out commands only if a condition is met?
74517.e: The “if ... then” block checks a condition. Only if it is true are the commands inside it carried out.
74517.m: With “if ... then” a program checks a condition.

74518.q: Program: “if points > 10 then say Great, else say Keep practising”. The variable points has the value 10. What does the sprite say?
74518.e: 10 is not greater than 10, so the condition is false. That is why the “else” part is carried out.
74518.m: If the condition is false, the “else” part is carried out.

74519.q: The variable x has the value 7. Which comparison is true?
74519.e: “>=” means “greater than or equal to”. As x is exactly 7, x >= 7 is true, while x > 7 is false.
74519.m: The sign “>=” includes the value itself.

74520.q: The condition is “(age > 9) and (age < 13)”. At which age is it true?
74520.e: With “and”, both parts must be true. Only 12 is greater than 9 and at the same time less than 13.
74520.m: With “and”, both conditions must be true.

74521.q: When is the condition “rain or snow” true?
a: When at least one of them applies
Only when it is exactly rain
74521.e: With “or”, it is enough if one of the two parts is true. It is also true if both apply.
74521.m: With “or”, one true condition is enough.

74522.e: 5 > 3 is true. “Not” reverses the truth value, so the result is false.
74522.m: The operator “not” swaps true and false.

74523.q: What do you call it when a program takes different paths depending on a condition?
74523.e: In branching, a condition decides which part of the program is carried out, for example with “if ... then ... else”.
74523.m: Branching lets a program choose between paths.

74524.q: What is a Boolean value in computer science?
a: A value that can only be true or false
74524.e: Boolean values only know true and false. They are named after the English mathematician George Boole and are needed for every condition.
74524.m: Boolean values are named after George Boole.

74525.q: What is a variable in programming?
a: A named storage place for a value
74525.e: A variable has a name and stores a value, for example the score in a game. The value can change.
74525.m: A variable stores a value under a name.

74526.q: Program: “set points to 5”, “change points by -2”, “change points by 4”. What value does points have?
74526.m: “Change by” adds to the old value.

74527.q: Program: a = 3, then b = a + 2, then a = 10. What value does b have at the end?
74527.e: b is calculated while a is still 3: 3 + 2 makes 5. The later change to a no longer changes b.
74527.m: A variable keeps its value until you give it a new one.

74528.q: You want to swap the values of two variables x and y. What do you need for this in most programming languages?
74528.e: First you store x in a temporary variable, then set x to y and finally y to the remembered value. Otherwise one value would be lost.
74528.m: To swap two values you need a temporary variable.

74529.q: What is the data type for text such as “Hello” called?
74529.e: Text is stored as a string. It is made up of a sequence of characters.
74529.m: Text is stored as a string.

74530.q: What does the statement “x = x + 1” do in Python?
74530.e: First x + 1 is calculated on the right, then the result is stored in x again. Here the equals sign means an assignment.
74530.m: In Python, the equals sign assigns a new value to a variable.

74531.q: What can you store in a list that a simple variable cannot store?
74531.e: A list contains many values one after the other, for example all the names in a class. Each entry has a position.
74531.m: A list stores several values in order.

74532.q: What does this Python program output: name = "Lea", then print("Hello " + name)?
74532.e: With texts, “+” joins the two parts together. Instead of “name”, the stored value “Lea” is put in.
74532.m: You can join texts together with the plus sign.

74533.q: Which block do you usually start a Scratch program with?
74533.e: A click on the green flag above the stage triggers this event and starts all scripts that begin with this block.
74533.m: The green flag starts Scratch programs.

74534.q: What do you call a kind of programming in which the program reacts to mouse clicks or key presses?
74534.e: In event-driven programming, parts of the program wait for an event and only start running when it happens.

74535.q: What does the Scratch block “broadcast message and wait” do?
a: It waits until all receiving scripts have finished
It always waits exactly one second
74535.e: The block sends the message like “broadcast message”, but only carries on once all the scripts that reacted to it have finished.
74535.m: “Broadcast and wait” waits for the receivers.

74536.q: How can a sprite in Scratch tell another sprite that it should do something?
74536.e: The “broadcast message” block sends a message. All scripts with “When I receive message” then start.
74536.m: In Scratch, sprites can communicate with messages.

74537.q: How can you recognise event blocks such as “When green flag clicked” in Scratch?
a: They are curved on top like a hat
They have a point at the bottom
74537.e: Event blocks are also called hat blocks. They have no notch on top, because they always come at the start of a script.
74537.m: Event blocks sit at the start of a script as hat blocks.

74538.q: In a Scratch game, the sprite should jump as soon as you press the space bar. Which block does the script start with?
74538.e: The block “When ... key pressed” reacts to a particular key. In it, you choose the space key.
74538.m: In Scratch, key presses trigger their own events.

74539.q: Two sprites each have a script that starts with “When green flag clicked”. What happens when you click the flag?
a: Both scripts start at the same time
The scripts start one after the other
74539.e: An event starts all the scripts waiting for that event. This way several sprites can act at the same time.
74539.m: One event can start many scripts at the same time.

74540.q: What does the red stop button above the stage do in Scratch?
74540.e: The red stop button ends all running scripts, including those with “forever”. The project is kept.
74540.m: In Scratch, the red button stops all scripts.

74541.q: A program is supposed to draw 10 stars but draws 11. What is this typical mistake called, where you miscount by exactly one?
74541.e: An off-by-one error often happens when a loop starts at 0 instead of 1 or ends with “less than or equal to” instead of “less than”.
74541.m: With loops it is easy to miscount by one.

74542.q: What is a test case in programming?
a: An input with the expected result
A mistake that only happens once
74542.e: With a test case you check whether the program gives the expected result for a particular input. If it differs, there is a mistake in the program.
74542.m: Test cases compare the result with the expected value.

74543.q: What did technicians find in the Harvard Mark II computer in 1947 that counts as the famous “first actual bug”?
74543.e: A moth was stuck in a relay. Grace Hopper's team taped it into the logbook with the note that it was the first actual case of a “bug” being found.
74543.m: The most famous computer bug was a real moth.

74544.q: In the Python code print("Hello" the closing bracket is missing. What kind of error is this?
74544.e: A syntax error breaks the writing rules of the programming language. That is why the program cannot even run.
74544.m: A syntax error breaks the writing rules of a language.

74545.q: A program runs without an error message but calculates 2 + 2 as 5. What kind of error is this?
