74945.m: Donghua Li became Olympic champion in artistic gymnastics in 1996.

74946.q: Why do gymnasts rub their hands with chalk?
a: For dry hands and a better grip
74946.e: Gymnastics chalk is a white powder that absorbs sweat. With dry hands you are less likely to slip off the horizontal bar, parallel bars or rings.
74946.m: Chalk keeps hands dry and gives a good grip.

74947.q: Which swimming stroke comes first in the individual medley?
74947.e: In the individual medley the order is butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke and freestyle. So you start with butterfly.
74947.m: The individual medley starts with butterfly.

74948.q: Which swimming stroke comes first in the medley relay?
74948.e: In the medley relay the first swimmer swims backstroke, because it starts in the water. Then come breaststroke, butterfly and freestyle.
74948.m: The medley relay starts with backstroke.

74949.q: In which competitive swimming stroke do you start in the water instead of from the starting block?
74949.e: At the start, backstroke swimmers hold on to the starting block and push off from the wall in the water. All the others dive from the block.
74949.m: In backstroke you start in the water.

74950.q: In which swimming stroke do both legs move up and down at the same time like a dolphin's tail?
74950.e: In butterfly you do the dolphin kick. Both legs stay together and move in a wave together.
74950.m: In butterfly both legs kick at the same time.

74951.q: Which medal did Swiss swimmer Noè Ponti win in the 100 m butterfly in Tokyo in 2021?
74951.e: Noè Ponti from Ticino won bronze in the 100 m butterfly at the Olympic Games in Tokyo.
74951.m: Noè Ponti won Olympic bronze in Tokyo in 2021.

74953.q: How many players per team are on the full-size court in floorball, including the goalkeeper?
74953.e: On the full-size court each team has five outfield players and one goalkeeper. That makes six people.
74953.m: In full-size floorball, six players per team are on at the same time.

74954.q: What does the goalkeeper in floorball not have?
74954.e: The floorball goalkeeper plays without a stick. They block the ball with their body and may catch it with their hands in the goal area.
74954.m: Floorball goalkeepers play without a stick.

74955.q: How long does a floorball match on the full-size court last?
74955.e: A full-size match consists of three periods of 20 minutes each. There are breaks in between.
74955.m: Floorball is played in three periods of 20 minutes.

74956.q: How many holes does an official floorball ball have?
74956.e: The floorball ball is made of plastic, is hollow and has 26 holes. It is very light and can therefore go very fast.

74957.q: The Swiss call it “Unihockey”. What is this sport called internationally?
74957.e: Internationally, Unihockey is called floorball. The world governing body is called the International Floorball Federation.

74958.q: In which sport did the Swiss women become world champions for the first time in 2005?
74958.e: The Swiss women's floorball team won their first world title in Singapore in 2005.
74958.m: The Swiss women's floorball team became world champions in 2005.

74959.q: What are outfield players not allowed to do in floorball?
a: Play the ball with their head
Play the ball with their stick
Hold the stick with both hands
74959.e: In floorball the ball must not be played with the head. This protects against dangerous situations with sticks at head height.
74959.m: In floorball headers are not allowed.

74960.q: How many players per team are on the court in indoor volleyball?
74960.e: In indoor volleyball each team has six players. Three are at the front by the net, three at the back.
74960.m: In indoor volleyball there are six players per team.

74961.q: Up to how many points is a normal set played in indoor volleyball?
74961.e: A set goes up to 25 points, but you need at least a 2-point lead. A deciding set only goes up to 15.
74961.m: A volleyball set goes up to 25 points.

74962.q: What is the playing position called that only plays at the back and wears a shirt in a different colour?
74962.e: The libero is a defence specialist. They are not allowed to attack or block and stand out because of their different shirt colour.
74962.m: The libero is the defence specialist with a different shirt colour.

74963.q: What is playing the ball with both forearms held together called?
74963.e: For a dig you put your forearms together and let the ball bounce off them. This is mainly how you receive low and hard balls.
74963.m: In volleyball you receive low balls with a dig.

74964.q: How high is the volleyball net for men?
74964.e: For men, the top of the net is at 2.43 metres. For women it is 2.24 metres.
74964.m: The men's volleyball net is 2.43 metres high.

74965.q: How many people play in a beach volleyball team?
74965.e: Beach volleyball is played on sand with only two people per team. That is why each person has to master all the techniques.
74965.m: In beach volleyball two people make a team.

74966.q: How many players per team are on the court in indoor handball, including the goalkeeper?
74966.e: Each team has six outfield players and one goalkeeper. That makes seven people.
74966.m: In handball seven players per team are on at the same time.

74967.q: How long does a handball match last for adults?
74967.e: A handball match consists of two halves of 30 minutes each. There is a break in between.
74967.m: A handball match lasts two times 30 minutes.

74968.q: What is the longest you may hold the ball in your hand in handball?
74968.e: A player may hold the ball for no more than three seconds, even when standing still. This keeps the game fast.
74968.m: You may hold the handball for no more than three seconds.

74969.q: From what distance from the goal is a penalty throw taken in handball?
74969.e: That is why the penalty throw is also called a seven-metre throw. The thrower stands alone in front of the goalkeeper.
74969.m: The handball penalty throw is taken from seven metres.

74970.q: How far is the goal area line from the goal in handball?
74970.e: The goal area reaches 6 metres out in front of the goal. Apart from the goalkeeper, players are not allowed to enter it.
74970.m: The handball goal area reaches six metres in front of the goal.

74971.q: How long does a suspension last in handball?
74971.e: With a suspension, the player has to leave the court for 2 minutes. During this time their team plays with one player fewer.
74971.m: A suspension in handball lasts two minutes.

74972.q: What colours is a control flag in orienteering?
74972.e: A control flag is divided diagonally into orange and white. This makes it easy to see in the forest.
74972.m: Orienteering controls are orange and white.

74973.q: Which scale is typical for orienteering maps?
74973.e: Orienteering maps usually have a scale of 1:15,000 or 1:10,000. So at 1:15,000, one centimetre on the map equals 150 metres.
74973.m: Orienteering maps are very detailed large-scale maps.

74974.q: What does the colour yellow mean on an orienteering map?
74974.e: Yellow stands for open land such as meadows or fields. Water is blue, dense forest is green.
74974.m: On an orienteering map yellow means open land.

74975.q: What do brown contour lines that are very close together on an orienteering map show?
74975.e: Contour lines join points of the same height. If they are close together, the ground rises steeply over a short distance.
74975.m: Contour lines close together show steep ground.

74976.q: Which Swiss orienteer won 23 world championship gold medals?
74976.e: Simone Niggli-Luder from the canton of Bern won a total of 23 world titles. She is considered one of the best orienteers of all time.
74976.m: Simone Niggli is one of the most successful orienteers in the world.

74977.q: What does it mean to “set the map” (orient the map)?
a: Turn the map so that it matches the terrain
74977.e: When you set the map, you turn it so that its north matches north in the terrain. Then directions on the map match those in nature.
74977.m: A set map points the same way as the terrain.

74978.q: Who runs the Youth and Sport (J+S) programme in Switzerland?
74978.e: Youth and Sport is the federal government's sports promotion programme. It is led by the Federal Office of Sport (BASPO) and carried out together with the cantons.
74978.m: Youth and Sport is a federal programme.

74979.q: Who is the Youth and Sport programme meant for?
74979.e: Youth and Sport promotes sport for children and young people aged 5 to 20, for example in clubs and camps.
74979.m: Youth and Sport promotes sport for children and young people.

74980.q: What must leaders of J+S courses have?
74980.e: Anyone who leads J+S courses needs leader training in that sport. This ensures the quality of the courses.

74981.q: How does Youth and Sport support sports clubs and camps?
74981.e: The federal government pays contributions to J+S courses and camps, and it trains the leaders. This makes sports activities for children cheaper.
74981.m: Youth and Sport supports clubs with money and training.

74982.q: In which place in Ticino does BASPO run a well-known youth sports centre?
74982.e: The Centro Sportivo Nazionale della Gioventù in Tenero on Lake Maggiore belongs to BASPO. Many sports camps for young people take place there.
74982.m: There is a national youth sports centre in Tenero.

74983.q: Which federal department is also responsible for sport?
a: The Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport
The Department of the Environment, Transport, Energy and Communications
74983.e: The Federal Office of Sport (BASPO) belongs to the DDPS, the Department of Defence, Civil Protection and Sport. The word sport is in the name.
74983.m: At federal level, sport belongs to the DDPS.

74984.q: What do Swiss wrestlers fight on?
74984.e: Swiss wrestling (Schwingen) takes place in a round ring filled with sawdust. The sawdust cushions the falls.
74984.m: Swiss wrestling takes place in sawdust.

74985.q: What is the winner of the Federal Wrestling and Alpine Festival called?
74985.e: The winner of the Federal Festival may call himself Schwingerkönig, the Wrestling King. It is the highest title in Swiss wrestling.
74985.m: The winner of the Federal Festival is the Wrestling King.

74986.q: Which animal does the winner of the big Swiss wrestling festival get as a prize?
74986.e: At the Federal Wrestling Festival, animals are given as prizes. The Wrestling King receives a bull, called a “Muni” in Swiss German.
74986.m: The Wrestling King gets a bull.

74987.q: When is a Swiss wrestling bout won?
a: When both of the opponent's shoulder blades touch the ground
When the opponent leaves the sawdust
When the opponent lets go of the shorts
74987.e: A bout is won when the opponent lies in the sawdust with both shoulder blades at the same time. The winner must keep his grip on the shorts.
74987.m: You win by putting your opponent on both shoulder blades.

74988.q: What fabric are Swiss wrestling shorts made of?
74988.e: The short wrestling shorts are made of Zwilch, a very tear-resistant, coarse fabric. The wrestlers hold on to them.
74988.m: Swiss wrestling shorts are made of tough Zwilch.

74989.q: Who became Wrestling King in Pratteln in 2022?
74989.e: Joel Wicki from the Entlebuch won the Federal Festival in Pratteln in 2022. In 2019 Christian Stucki had won in Zug.
74989.m: Joel Wicki became Wrestling King in 2022.

74990.q: What does the winner traditionally do after a Swiss wrestling bout?
a: He brushes the sawdust off the loser's back
He shakes the sawdust over the audience
He takes off the wrestling shorts
74990.e: After the bout, the winner shakes the loser's hand and brushes the sawdust off his back. This shows respect and fairness.
74990.m: Fairness is part of the tradition in Swiss wrestling.

74991.q: How can you tell an easy endurance pace when jogging?
a: You can still have a conversation
You have to stop after a minute
You sprint as fast as possible
74991.e: At an easy base pace the body works aerobically. You breathe calmly enough to still speak in full sentences.
74991.m: At an easy endurance pace you can still chat.

74992.q: Which organ takes in oxygen from the air during sport?
74992.e: In the lungs, oxygen passes from the air you breathe into the blood. The blood then carries it to the muscles.
74992.m: The lungs take oxygen from the air.

74993.q: Besides carbohydrates, which energy source does the body use especially heavily during long, easy endurance exercise?
74993.e: During long efforts at a calm pace, the muscle burns a lot of fat with oxygen. Fat is a large energy store in the body.
74993.m: During long, easy exercise the body burns a lot of fat.

75037.q: Why shouldn't you put ice directly on the skin for a sports injury?
a: It can cause cold damage to the skin
75037.e: Direct contact with ice can cause local frostbite. That is why you put a cloth between the ice and the skin.
75037.m: Always put a cloth between the ice and your skin.

75038.q: Which emergency number do you call in Switzerland for an ambulance?
75038.e: 144 alerts the ambulance service. 117 is the police, 118 the fire brigade and 1414 Rega.
75038.m: In Switzerland you call an ambulance on 144.

75039.q: What is the emergency number of Rega, the Swiss air rescue service?
75039.e: Rega is alerted on 1414, for example for accidents in the mountains. From abroad you can reach it on +41 333 333 333.

75042.q: What is the right thing to do for a heavy nosebleed after being hit by a ball?
a: Lean your head forward and pinch the sides of your nose
75042.e: With your head forward, the blood flows out of your nose instead of into your throat. Cooling the back of your neck also helps.
75042.m: For a nosebleed, lean your head forward.

75094.q: Which family of instruments does the violin belong to?
75094.e: On a violin you draw a bow across the strings. That is why it belongs to the string instruments.
75094.m: The violin is a string instrument.

75095.q: Which family of instruments does the piano belong to?
75095.e: On a piano you press keys to play a note. That is why it counts as a keyboard instrument.
75095.m: The piano is a keyboard instrument.

75096.q: Which family of instruments does the guitar belong to?
75096.e: The strings of a guitar are plucked with the fingers. That is why it is a plucked instrument.
75096.m: The guitar is a plucked instrument.

75097.q: Which family of instruments does the clarinet belong to?
75097.e: The clarinet is made of wood and has a reed on the mouthpiece. It belongs to the woodwind instruments.
75097.m: The clarinet is a woodwind instrument.

75098.q: The saxophone is made of metal. Which family does it still belong to?
75098.e: The saxophone has a reed, like the clarinet. That is why it counts as a woodwind instrument.
75098.m: Because of its reed, the saxophone is a woodwind instrument.

75099.q: Which family of instruments does the xylophone belong to?
75099.e: On a xylophone you strike wooden bars with beaters. That is why it belongs to the percussion instruments.
75099.m: The xylophone is a percussion instrument with wooden bars.

75100.q: Which family of instruments does the French horn belong to?
75100.e: The French horn is made of brass, and the sound is made by the lips on the mouthpiece. It is a brass instrument.
75100.m: The French horn is a brass instrument.

75101.q: Which instrument is a percussion instrument?
75101.e: The triangle is a bent metal bar that you strike with a small rod. That is why it is a percussion instrument.
75101.m: The triangle is a small metal percussion instrument.

75102.q: Which large keyboard instrument in church has lots of pipes?
75102.e: On an organ, air flows through pipes when you press the keys. You often find one in churches.
75102.m: The organ is a keyboard instrument with many pipes.

75103.q: What is volume called in music?
75103.e: In music, dynamics means how loudly or quietly something is played.
75103.m: Volume in music is called dynamics.

75104.e: Decrescendo comes from Italian and means decreasing. So the music gets quieter bit by bit.
75104.m: In a decrescendo the music gradually gets quieter.

75105.q: What does the sign “ff” mean in written music?
75105.e: The abbreviation ff stands for fortissimo. That means you play very loudly.
75105.m: The sign ff means you play very loudly.

75106.q: What does the sign “mf” mean in written music?
75106.e: The abbreviation mf stands for mezzo forte. Mezzo means half, so you play moderately loudly.
75106.m: The sign mf means moderately loud.

75107.q: Why was the piano once called the “pianoforte”?
a: It can play quietly and loudly
75107.e: Piano means quiet and forte means loud. On a pianoforte the volume depends on how hard you strike the key.
75107.m: The pianoforte can play quietly and loudly.

75108.q: What do you put into a trumpet to make it sound quieter?
75108.e: A mute is put into the bell at the front. It makes the sound quieter and changes it.
75108.m: A mute makes a trumpet quieter.

75109.q: How do you play a quiet note on a drum?
75109.e: The more gently you hit the skin, the less it vibrates. That is why the note sounds quieter.
75109.m: Hitting a drum gently plays it quietly.

75110.q: Which word describes how high or low a note is?
75110.e: Pitch tells you whether a note sounds high or low.
75110.m: Whether a note is high or low is called its pitch.

75111.e: Large bells vibrate more slowly than small ones. That is why they sound lower.
75111.m: Large bells sound lower than small ones.

75112.q: Which bars on a xylophone sound higher?
75112.e: Short bars vibrate faster than long ones. That is why they sound higher.
75112.m: On a xylophone the short bars sound higher.

75113.q: Which pipes of a panpipe sound lowest?
75113.e: More air vibrates in a long pipe. That is why the note sounds lower.
75113.m: On a panpipe the long pipes sound low.

75114.q: What happens to the note of a guitar string when you tighten it?
75114.e: A tightly stretched string vibrates faster. That is why it sounds higher.
75114.m: The tighter a string is, the higher it sounds.

75115.e: The bassoon has a very long, folded tube. That is why it sounds low.
75115.m: The bassoon is a low woodwind instrument.

75116.q: Which animal has a very high voice?
75116.e: The mouse is small and squeaks in a high voice. Big animals like bears, cows and lions growl, moo or roar deeply.
75116.m: The little mouse squeaks in a high voice.

75117.e: Small birds chirp with bright, high notes. Thunder, engines and large bells sound low.

75118.e: Allegro is Italian and means cheerful. In music it means a fast, lively tempo.

75119.e: Adagio is Italian and means at ease. So you play slowly.

75120.e: Presto means quick in Italian. In music it is one of the fastest tempos.

75121.e: Accelerando means speeding up. The tempo gets faster bit by bit.
75121.m: In an accelerando the music gradually gets faster.

75122.e: Ritardando means holding back. The tempo gets slower bit by bit, often at the end of a piece.
75122.m: In a ritardando the music gradually gets slower.

75123.e: Andante comes from the Italian word for walking. The tempo is calm, like a gentle stroll.
75123.m: Andante means a calm, walking tempo.

75124.q: What does the number 120 on a metronome show?
75124.e: A metronome counts beats per minute. At 120 it ticks once every half second.
75124.m: The number on a metronome shows the beats per minute.

75125.q: Which famous, very fast piece of music imitates a flying insect?
75125.e: “Flight of the Bumblebee” is by the Russian composer Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. The fast notes sound like the buzzing of a bumblebee.
75125.m: Flight of the Bumblebee is a very fast piece of music.

75126.q: How many beats does a minim (half note) last in 4/4 time?
75126.e: A semibreve (whole note) lasts 4 beats. The minim lasts half as long, so 2 beats.

75127.q: How many crotchets (quarter notes) last as long as a minim (half note)?
75127.e: A crotchet lasts 1 beat, a minim 2 beats. So you need 2 crotchets.
75127.m: Two crotchets last as long as a minim.

75128.q: What does a crotchet (quarter note) look like?
75128.e: The crotchet has a filled-in black note head and a stem without a tail.
75128.m: The crotchet has a black head and a stem.

75129.q: What does a minim (half note) look like?
75129.e: The minim has an empty white note head and a stem.
75129.m: The minim has a white head and a stem.

75130.q: Which note has a white head and no stem?
75130.e: The semibreve is just an empty oval head without a stem.

75131.q: Which note has a small tail on its stem?
75131.e: The quaver looks like a crotchet with a tail. Two quavers are often joined with a beam.
75131.m: You can recognise a quaver by its tail.

75132.q: What is the rest called that lasts as long as a minim (half note)?
75132.e: Every note has a matching rest of the same length. So the minim rest lasts two beats and looks like a little hat sitting on the line.
75132.m: The minim rest lasts as long as a minim.

75133.q: How long does a crotchet (quarter) rest last?
75133.e: A crotchet rest lasts exactly as long as a crotchet, so one beat.
75133.m: A crotchet rest lasts one beat.

a: At the start of the stave
At the end of the stave
75134.e: The clef is right at the front of every stave. It shows which note sits on which line.
75134.m: The clef is at the start of every stave.

75135.q: Which clef is used for low notes?
75135.e: The bass clef is used for low instruments such as the cello, the tuba or the left hand on the piano.
75135.m: The bass clef is used for low notes.

75136.q: What are the short lines above or below the five lines of the stave called?
75136.e: For very high or very low notes you draw short ledger lines above or below the stave.
75136.m: Ledger lines help with very high and very low notes.

75137.e: A note head can sit on a line or in the space between two lines. That gives more room for different notes.
75137.m: Notes sit on the lines or in the spaces.

75138.q: How many spaces are there between the five lines of the stave?
75138.e: Between five lines there is always one space fewer than lines, so 4 spaces.
75138.m: There are four spaces between the five lines of the stave.

75139.q: Which line of the stave counts as the first line?
75139.e: The lines of the stave are counted from the bottom up. So the bottom line is the first.
75139.m: The lines of the stave are counted from the bottom up.

75140.q: In the treble clef, which note sits on the first ledger line below the five lines?
75140.e: In the treble clef, C sits on a small ledger line below the stave. The C major scale often starts on it.
75140.m: The low C in the treble clef sits on a ledger line.

75141.q: What is the double line at the very end of a piece of music called?
75141.e: A final double bar line is made of one thin and one thick line. It shows the end of the piece.
75141.m: The final double bar line shows the end of a piece of music.

75142.q: Which animal appears in the song “Det äne am Bergli”?
75142.e: In this Swiss folk song a white goat stands over on the hill. The farmer wants to milk it.
75142.m: The song “Det äne am Bergli” is about a white goat.

75143.q: What does the goat in the song “Det äne am Bergli” do when the farmer wants to milk it?
75143.e: When the farmer wants to milk the white goat, it kicks him. That is what this funny Swiss folk song tells.
75143.m: In the song the white goat kicks the farmer.

75144.q: What weather does the song “Es schneielet, es beielet” tell of?
75144.e: This Swiss German song describes a snowstorm in winter. “Schneielet” means that it is snowing in Swiss German.
75144.m: The song “Es schneielet, es beielet” is a winter song.

75145.q: Who do Swiss children often welcome with the song “What’s that little light?”
75145.e: Children in Switzerland sing this song, “Was isch das für es Liechtli”, to welcome Samichlaus, who visits at the beginning of December.
75145.m: The “little light” song is sung to welcome Samichlaus.

75146.q: What do the Ramseyers want to do in the well-known Bernese folk song?
75146.e: In the song “Ramseyers wei go grase” the family wants to mow grass. The song is set on the Gümligenberg near Bern.
75146.m: In the song the Ramseyers want to go and cut grass.

75147.q: What is the girl in the Guggisberg song called?
75147.e: The old Bernese song is also called “S Vreneli ab em Guggisbärg”. It is one of the oldest known Swiss folk songs.
75147.m: The Guggisberg song tells of Vreneli.

75148.q: Which mountain does the journey in the song “Vo Luzärn uf Wäggis zue” lead to?
75148.e: The song is also called the Rigi song. It tells of a trip from Lucerne via Weggis up the Rigi.
75148.m: The Rigi song goes from Lucerne via Weggis up the Rigi.

75149.q: What are songs sung in Swiss German called?
75149.e: A dialect is the language people speak every day in a region. Songs in Swiss German are therefore called dialect songs.
75149.m: Songs in Swiss German are called dialect songs.

a: A pattern of long and short notes
75150.e: A rhythm is made when long and short notes and rests follow each other in a particular order.
75150.m: A rhythm is a pattern of long and short notes.

75151.q: What do you call music made by clapping, stamping and clicking your fingers?
75151.e: In body percussion your own body is the instrument. You clap, stamp, click your fingers or pat your thighs.
75151.m: In body percussion you make music with your own body.

75152.q: How many times do you clap when you clap the word “pineapple” in syllables?
75152.e: The word has the syllables pine, ap and ple. You clap once for each syllable, so 3 times.
75152.m: You clap once for each syllable of a word.

75153.q: What do you do in echo clapping?
75153.e: One person claps a rhythm, and the others clap it back exactly the same. This is how you practise rhythms.
75153.m: In echo clapping you clap a rhythm back exactly.

75154.q: Which beat in a bar is usually stressed most strongly?
75154.e: The first beat after the bar line is called the downbeat. It is usually stressed most strongly.
75154.m: The first beat in a bar is usually stressed most strongly.

75155.q: Which wooden box do you sit on and drum with your hands?
75155.e: The cajón comes from Peru. You sit on it and hit the wooden front panel with your hands.
75155.m: The cajón is a box you sit on and drum.

75156.q: Which music is good for marching in step to?
75156.e: A march has a steady, even rhythm. You can walk in step to it.
75156.m: You walk in step to a march.

75157.q: Which wooden rhythm instruments do you strike against each other?
75157.e: Claves are two round wooden sticks. When you strike them together, they make a bright, short sound.
75157.m: Claves are struck against each other.

75158.q: What do you have to do with a rattle to make it sound?
75158.e: A rattle has small seeds or beads inside. When you shake it, they bounce against the sides and rattle.
75158.m: A rattle sounds when you shake it.

75159.q: What is the lower voice of women and children in a choir called?
75159.e: In a choir, women and children sing either the high soprano or the somewhat lower alto.
75159.m: The alto is the lower female voice in a choir.

75160.q: What is the high male voice in a choir called?
75160.e: Among the men, the tenor sings higher and the bass lower.
75160.m: The tenor is the high male voice.

75161.q: Why does a choir warm up before rehearsal?
a: To learn the words by heart
75161.e: When warming up, the voice is warmed up like a muscle. This helps you sing more cleanly and protects your voice.
75161.m: Warming up gets your voice ready to sing.

75162.e: A cappella means only voices can be heard. No instruments accompany the singing.
75162.m: A cappella means singing without instruments.

75163.q: What is it called when you sing a melody with your mouth closed?
75163.e: When you hum, your lips stay closed. The sound comes through your nose and is soft.
75163.m: When you hum, you sing with your mouth closed.

75164.q: What is it called when a choir sings different notes at the same time?
75164.e: When the groups in a choir sing different notes at the same time, you get a sound in several parts.
75164.m: A choir sings in parts when different notes sound at the same time.

75165.q: How should you breathe when singing?
75165.e: Singing needs a lot of air. If you breathe deep into your belly, the air lasts for longer notes.
75165.m: To sing, breathe deep into your belly.

75166.q: Which city is the famous boys’ choir that has existed for over 500 years from?
75166.e: The Vienna Boys Choir was founded in 1498. It sings on concert tours all over the world.
75166.m: The Vienna Boys Choir is a famous boys’ choir from Vienna.

75167.q: What is the old turning dance in three time from the Alpine region called?
75167.e: The Ländler is a couple dance from the Alps. The waltz later developed from it.
75167.m: The Ländler is an old dance from the Alps.

75168.q: What do many folk dance groups in Switzerland wear when they perform?
75168.e: Traditional costume is the traditional clothing of a region. Folk dance groups often wear it at festivals.
75168.m: Folk dancers often wear traditional costume.

75169.q: Which region does the polka come from?
75169.e: The polka began in the 19th century in Bohemia, which is now part of the Czech Republic. It is a lively couple dance.

75170.q: In which dance do men slap their shoes and thighs with their hands?
75170.e: The Schuhplattler is a folk dance from Bavaria and Tyrol. The dancers slap the soles of their shoes, their knees and their thighs.
75170.m: In the Schuhplattler the dancers slap their shoes and thighs.

75171.q: Which country does flamenco come from?
75171.e: Flamenco comes from Andalusia in the south of Spain. Typical features are guitar, clapping and stamping.

75172.q: Which country does the sirtaki dance come from?
75172.e: The sirtaki became famous through the film “Zorba the Greek”. It is danced in a line, with arms on the neighbours’ shoulders.
75172.m: The sirtaki is a dance from Greece.

75173.q: Which country does the tarantella come from?
75173.e: The tarantella is a fast folk dance from southern Italy.
75173.m: The tarantella is a fast dance from Italy.

75174.q: Which country does the csárdás come from?
75174.e: The csárdás is a Hungarian dance. It often starts slowly and then becomes very fast.
75174.m: The csárdás is a dance from Hungary.

75175.q: Which wood is an alphorn traditionally made from?
75175.e: In the past, spruce trees that had grown crooked were used for alphorns. Spruce wood is still typical today.
75175.m: An alphorn is traditionally made of spruce wood.

75176.q: Roughly how long is an alphorn in Switzerland?
75176.e: The alphorn in F sharp, common in Switzerland, is about 3.47 metres long.
75176.m: A Swiss alphorn is about three and a half metres long.

75177.q: How do you make the different notes on an alphorn?
75177.e: The alphorn has no keys and no finger holes. You make the different notes only with your lips.
75177.m: On an alphorn you make all the notes with your lips alone.

75178.q: How many parts can an alphorn usually be taken apart into?
75178.e: An alphorn can usually be taken apart into three pieces. That makes it easier to carry.
75178.m: An alphorn can usually be taken apart into three pieces.

75179.q: What did herders in the mountains use the alphorn for in the past?
a: As a signal over long distances
75179.e: The sound of the alphorn carries very far. That is why it was once used as a signalling instrument in the mountains.
75179.m: In the past the alphorn was used as a signal in the mountains.

75180.q: What is the mouthpiece of an alphorn usually made of?
75180.e: The mouthpiece of an alphorn is usually turned from wood. You blow into it as with a trumpet.
75180.m: The mouthpiece of an alphorn is usually made of wood.

75181.q: What do you press on a Schwyzerörgeli to play notes?
75181.e: The Schwyzerörgeli has no piano keys, but round buttons in several rows.
75181.m: On a Schwyzerörgeli you play on buttons.

75182.q: What is the part of the Schwyzerörgeli called that you pull apart and push together?
75182.e: The bellows are like a folding wall. They blow air through the reeds so that notes are made.
75182.m: On a Schwyzerörgeli you move the bellows in and out.

75183.q: What is special about the Schwyzerörgeli when you pull or push the bellows?
a: One button gives two different notes
75183.e: The melody side is bisonoric. The same button gives a different note when pulling than when pushing.
75183.m: On a Schwyzerörgeli one button gives different notes when pulling and pushing.

75184.q: Which type of instrument is the Schwyzerörgeli?
75184.e: The Schwyzerörgeli is a kind of accordion with buttons.

75185.q: What is the first violinist in an orchestra called?
75185.e: The leader sits at the first desk of the first violins and leads the string players.
75185.m: The leader is the first violinist in the orchestra.

75186.q: Where do the percussion instruments usually sit in an orchestra?
75186.e: Percussion instruments are loud. That is why they are usually right at the back of the orchestra.
75186.m: Percussion instruments are usually at the back of the orchestra.

75187.q: What is the conductor’s big music book with all the parts called?
75187.e: In the score the parts of all the instruments are written one below the other. That way the conductor sees everything at a glance.
75187.m: The score contains all the parts of an orchestral piece.

75188.q: What is the string instrument called that is a bit bigger and lower than the violin?
75188.e: The viola is held like a violin, but it sounds somewhat lower.
75188.m: The viola is a bit bigger and lower than the violin.

75189.q: Where does the orchestra usually play in an opera house?
75189.e: The orchestra pit is lower down in front of the stage. That way the audience can see the singers well.
75189.m: At the opera the orchestra plays in the orchestra pit.

75190.q: Which instrument plays the bird in “Peter and the Wolf”?
75190.e: In this piece by Sergei Prokofiev each character has its own instrument. The bird twitters on the flute.
75190.m: In “Peter and the Wolf” the flute plays the bird.

75191.q: Which instrument plays the grandfather in “Peter and the Wolf”?
75191.e: The bassoon sounds low and a little grumpy. That is why it suits the grumpy grandfather.
75191.m: In “Peter and the Wolf” the bassoon plays the grandfather.

75192.q: What do you call a small orchestra with only a few musicians?
75192.e: A chamber orchestra is smaller than a symphony orchestra. In the past it played in the chambers, meaning the rooms, of princes.
75192.m: A small orchestra is called a chamber orchestra.

75193.q: In which Swiss city does the KKL concert hall stand right by the lake?
75193.e: The Lucerne Culture and Convention Centre (KKL) is on Lake Lucerne. Famous orchestras from all over the world play there.
75193.m: The KKL is a famous concert hall in Lucerne.

75194.q: A crotchet (quarter note) is divided entirely into semiquavers (sixteenth notes). How many semiquavers does that make?
75194.e: A crotchet equals two quavers, and each quaver equals two semiquavers. So 2 times 2 makes exactly 4 semiquavers.
75194.m: A crotchet lasts as long as four semiquavers.

75195.q: How many tails does a single semiquaver (sixteenth note) have?
75195.e: The quaver has one tail, the semiquaver two. Each extra tail halves the length of the note.
75195.m: Each extra tail halves the length of a note.

75196.q: What do you call three notes that together last as long as two notes of the same value?
75196.e: In a triplet, three notes are played in the time of two of the same notes. It is marked with a small 3.
75196.m: A triplet squeezes three notes into the time of two.

75197.q: What is the line called that joins several quavers (eighth notes) together?
75197.e: Instead of giving each quaver its own tail, several are joined with a beam. This makes the beats in the bar easier to read.
75197.m: A beam joins several quavers into a group.

75198.q: Where is the semibreve (whole) rest written on the stave?
a: It hangs below the fourth line
It sits on the third line
It hangs below the first line
It sits on the fifth line
75198.e: The semibreve rest is a small block hanging from the fourth line. The minim rest looks similar but sits on the third line.
75198.m: The semibreve rest hangs, the minim rest sits.

75199.q: What does a tie between two notes of the same pitch do?
a: The note values are added together
The notes are played an octave higher
75199.e: With a tie you play the note only once and hold it as long as both notes together. This way a note can also sound across a bar line.
75199.m: A tie lengthens a note by the value of the second note.

75200.q: Which time signature with two crotchet beats per bar is typical for marches?
75200.e: A march fits walking with two steps: left, right. That is why many marches are in 2/4 time.
75200.m: Many marches are in 2/4 time, matching the steps.

75201.q: A piece is in 5/4 time. How many crotchet beats do you count in each bar?
75201.e: The top number 5 gives the number of beats, and the bottom number 4 says that each beat is a crotchet. A well-known example is the jazz piece “Take Five”.
75201.m: In 5/4 time you count five crotchets per bar.

75202.q: What does the top number of a time signature tell you?
a: How many beats a bar has
75202.e: The top number shows the number of beats per bar. In 3/4 time there are three beats.
75202.m: The top number of a time signature counts the beats in a bar.

75203.q: How many main beats is a fast 6/8 time usually counted in?
75203.e: The six quavers form two groups of three quavers each. At a fast tempo you therefore count only two main beats, which are dotted crotchets.
75203.m: A fast 6/8 time swings in two big beats.

75204.q: Which time signature is called “alla breve”?
75204.e: Alla breve means you count in minims rather than crotchets. The sign is a C with a vertical line through it.
75204.m: In alla breve time you count two minims per bar.

75205.q: In pop and jazz in 4/4 time, which beats do people usually clap on?
75205.e: In pop, rock and jazz the snare drum beats often fall on two and four. This rhythm is called the backbeat.
75205.m: With the backbeat you clap on two and four.

75206.q: Which clef is also called the F clef?
75206.e: The bass clef developed from the letter F. Its two dots surround the line on which the F below middle C sits.
75206.m: The bass clef is also called the F clef.

75207.q: Which instrument is usually written in the bass clef?
75207.e: The cello plays low notes, so its music is usually written in the bass clef. Flute, trumpet and violin use the treble clef.
75207.m: Low instruments like the cello read the bass clef.

75208.q: In the treble clef, which note sits in the bottom space?
75208.e: The bottom line in the treble clef is E, the second line G. So F sits in the space between them.
75208.m: From the bottom, the spaces in the treble clef spell F, A, C, E.

75209.q: In the bass clef, which note sits on the top line?
75209.e: The top line in the bass clef carries the A below middle C. Directly below it is the line with F.
75209.m: The top line in the bass clef is A.

75210.q: Which notes make up the C major triad?
75210.e: You stack two thirds on the root C: C to E is a major third, E to G a minor third.
75210.m: The C major triad is made of C, E and G.

75211.q: Which major key has exactly one flat in its key signature?
75211.e: In the F major scale, B is lowered to B flat so that there is a semitone between the 3rd and 4th notes. That is why F major has one flat.
75211.m: F major is the major key with one flat.

75212.q: How does a song in a minor key usually sound compared with a major key?
75212.e: Major often sounds bright and cheerful, minor rather dark, sad or serious. This is mainly due to the minor third in a minor key.
75212.m: Minor usually sounds darker and sadder than major.

75213.q: Which note turns the C major triad (C, E, G) into a C minor triad?
75213.e: Major and minor differ in the third. In C minor, E is lowered by a semitone to E flat. C major and C minor share the same keynote and are called parallel keys.
75213.m: The third decides whether a triad is major or minor.

75215.q: What is the interval between two notes of the same pitch called?
75215.e: It is also called the prime, from the Latin word for “the first”. Both notes are on the same step.
75215.m: Two identical notes form a unison.

75216.q: What is the interval from C up to G called?
75216.e: You count the steps C, D, E, F, G and get five. Five steps make a fifth.
75216.m: An interval spanning five steps is called a fifth.

75217.q: What is the interval from C up to F called?
75217.e: From C to F you count four steps: C, D, E, F. Four steps make a fourth.
75217.m: An interval spanning four steps is called a fourth.

75218.q: How many semitones make up a major third?
75218.e: A major third is made of two whole tones, for example C to E. Two whole tones make four semitones.
75218.m: A major third spans four semitones.

75219.q: How many semitones make up a minor third?
75219.e: A minor third is made of one whole tone and one semitone, for example A to C. That makes three semitones.
75219.m: A minor third spans three semitones.

75220.q: Which interval do you hear in the first two notes of “Somewhere Over the Rainbow”?
75220.e: On “Some-where” the melody leaps from the first note to the note of the same name eight steps higher. This song helps many people recognise the octave.
75220.m: Well-known song openings help you recognise intervals.

75221.q: Which interval do you hear in the first two notes of “O Tannenbaum” (O Christmas Tree)?
75221.e: The song begins with a leap of four steps upwards, for example from D to G. That is a fourth.

75222.q: How big is the distance between the notes E and F?
75222.e: On the piano there is no black key between E and F. So the two notes are right next to each other, a semitone apart.
75222.m: Between E and F, and between B and C, there is only a semitone.

75223.q: What does the marking “sforzando” (sfz) ask for on a note?
a: To accent it suddenly and strongly
75223.e: Sforzando means “forced” in Italian. The single note is made to stand out with a strong accent.
75223.m: With sforzando a note is suddenly strongly accented.

75224.q: What does the marking “fp” (fortepiano) ask for?
a: Start loud and immediately become quiet
75224.e: With fortepiano the note is struck strongly and then immediately drops back to quiet. This creates a surprising effect.
75224.m: Fortepiano starts loud and immediately becomes quiet.

75225.q: What does a hairpin under the notes that opens to the right show?
a: That the tempo stays the same
75225.e: The wider the hairpin opens, the louder you should play. A hairpin that closes to the right means getting quieter.
75225.m: An opening hairpin means increasing volume.

75226.q: Which language do most dynamic markings in music come from?
75226.e: In the 17th and 18th centuries Italy was very influential in music. That is why Italian terms are still used for volume today.
75226.m: Volume markings in music are mostly Italian.

75227.q: What does an accent mark “>” above a note mean?
75227.e: The sign looks like a small point and shows an accent. The note stands out more than the notes around it.
75227.m: An accent makes a single note stand out.

75228.q: Which of these tempo markings is the slowest?
75228.e: Largo means “broad” and stands for a very slow tempo. Andante is faster, Allegro and Presto faster still.
75228.m: Largo is a very slow, broad tempo.

75229.q: What does the marking “a tempo” mean after a change of tempo?
75229.e: After a ritardando or accelerando, “a tempo” shows that you continue in the earlier basic tempo.
75229.m: With “a tempo” you return to the basic tempo.

75230.q: Which male voice lies between tenor and bass?
75230.e: The baritone is the middle male voice. It sounds lower than the tenor and higher than the bass.
75230.m: The baritone lies between tenor and bass.

75231.q: Which female voice lies between soprano and alto?
75231.e: Mezzo is Italian for “half” or “middle”. So the mezzo-soprano lies in the middle between soprano and alto.
75231.m: The mezzo-soprano is the middle female voice.

75232.q: What does the abbreviation SATB stand for in a choir?
75232.e: SATB names the four voices of a mixed choir. The order goes from the highest to the lowest voice.
75232.m: A mixed choir usually sings in the four voices soprano, alto, tenor and bass.

75233.q: What do you call a male singer who sings in the alto range using his head voice?
75233.e: The countertenor sings very high with a specially trained head voice. This voice type is especially popular in Baroque music.
75233.m: A countertenor sings in the alto range with his head voice.

75234.q: What do you call a high soprano who is especially good at singing fast runs and ornaments?
75234.e: Coloratura means fast, ornamented runs of notes. A coloratura soprano specialises in such virtuoso passages.
75234.m: A coloratura soprano sings high, fast ornaments.

75235.q: What do you call the span from the lowest to the highest note a voice can sing?
75235.e: The vocal range shows how many notes a voice can reach. It helps find the right voice type for a person.
75235.m: The vocal range goes from the lowest to the highest note you can sing.

75236.q: What do the small numbers above the notes of a round show?
a: Where the next voice comes in
75236.e: The first group starts at number 1. When it reaches number 2, the second group starts from the beginning, and so on.
75236.m: The numbers in a round mark where the voices come in.

75237.q: Which of these German songs is a well-known round?
75237.e: “Froh zu sein bedarf es wenig” is often sung by groups one after another. The other songs are normally sung in unison.
75237.m: A round only works if the melody fits with itself.

75238.q: What is the French original of the round known in English as “Are You Sleeping, Brother John?”?
75238.e: “Frère Jacques” is an old French children’s song. It has been translated into many languages and is sung as a round all over the world.
75238.m: “Brother John” comes from France, where it is called “Frère Jacques”.

75239.q: What do all the groups sing in a round?
a: The same melody, but starting at different times
All the same note at the same time
75239.e: In a round one group starts and the next ones come in later with the same melody. This creates several parts. A famous example of a canon is the one by Johann Pachelbel.
75239.m: In a round everyone sings the same melody one after another.

75240.q: What is the smallest number of groups needed for a round to sound in parts?
75240.e: Even with two groups starting at different times, two voices sound at once. Many rounds are written for three or four groups.
75240.m: A round needs at least two voices.

75241.q: How does the melody of “Brother John” sound when played in a minor key?
a: Exactly the same as in major
75241.e: Minor usually sounds darker than major. The composer Gustav Mahler even turned “Brother John” in minor into a funeral march in his 1st Symphony.
75241.m: In a minor key even a cheerful song sounds sad.

75242.q: What do you call a round that can start again from the beginning over and over?
75242.e: In a perpetual canon the end of the melody leads seamlessly back to the beginning. So it can be repeated as often as you like.
75242.m: A perpetual canon goes round and round like a wheel.

75243.q: Which Latin round asking for peace is often sung by choirs?
75243.e: “Dona nobis pacem” means “Give us peace”. This three-part round is widely sung in schools and choirs.
75243.m: “Dona nobis pacem” is a well-known round for peace.

75244.e: Johann Strauss II composed a great many waltzes in 19th-century Vienna. They made him world-famous.
75244.m: Johann Strauss II is the famous Waltz King.

75245.q: What is the best-known waltz by Johann Strauss II called?
75245.e: The Blue Danube waltz was written in 1867 and is seen as Austria’s unofficial anthem. It is played every year at the New Year’s Concert in Vienna.
75245.m: The Blue Danube is the most famous waltz from Vienna.

75246.q: Which waltz is the faster dance?
75246.e: The Viennese waltz is danced at about 60 bars per minute, the slow waltz at only about 30. That is why you turn much faster in the Viennese waltz.
75246.m: The Viennese waltz is much faster than the slow waltz.

75247.q: What is the slow waltz also called?
75247.e: The slow waltz developed in England. That is why it is also called the English waltz.
75247.m: The slow waltz is also called the English waltz.

75248.q: In which two cities on the Río de la Plata did the tango begin?
a: Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo
75248.e: The tango began at the end of the 19th century in the harbour districts of both cities. Many immigrants brought influences from Europe and Africa.
75248.m: The tango comes from the port cities on the Río de la Plata.

75249.q: Which bellows instrument shapes the sound of Argentine tango?
75249.e: The bandoneon was invented in Germany and reached South America with emigrants. There it became the typical tango instrument.
75249.m: The bandoneon is the heart of the tango.

75250.q: In which country is the tango seen as the typical national dance?
75250.e: The tango began in Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Especially in Argentina it is still a symbol of the country today.
75250.m: The tango is the typical dance of Argentina.

75251.q: What kind of dance is the tango?
75251.e: In the tango two people dance close together. One leads, the other follows.
75251.m: The tango is danced in pairs.

75252.e: The B stands for “break”, the part of a song people danced to. The dancers themselves often call their dance “breaking”.
75252.m: Breakdancers are called B-girls and B-boys.

75253.q: In which hip-hop dance style do you tense your muscles sharply so that your body seems to twitch?
75253.e: In popping, muscles are briefly tensed and released in time with the beat. This creates a robot-like, twitching effect.
75253.m: In popping the muscles twitch to the beat of the music.

75254.q: What is the breakdance move called in which you spin on your head?
75254.e: In a headspin the dancer balances on her head and spins like a top. Dancers often wear a hat or helmet for it.
75254.m: In a headspin you spin on your head.

75255.q: At which Olympic Games was breaking an Olympic event for the first time?
75255.e: Breaking made its Olympic debut at the 2024 Summer Games in Paris. It was not included in the programme for Los Angeles 2028.
75255.m: Breaking was Olympic for the first time in Paris in 2024.

75256.q: What do you call a small band that plays traditional Swiss dance music?
75256.e: A Ländler band often has a Schwyzerörgeli or accordion, clarinet, piano and double bass. It plays Ländler, schottische, polka and waltz.
75256.m: A Ländler band plays traditional Swiss dance music.

75257.q: What do you call a yodel sung entirely without words?
75257.e: In a Naturjodel you only sing syllables like “jo-ho-di”, but no text. A well-known example is the Appenzell Zäuerli.

75258.q: What is spun round in a clay bowl in the Appenzell Talerschwingen?
75258.e: In Talerschwingen a coin, usually a five-franc piece, is made to roll round and round in a clay bowl. This makes a long, humming sound that accompanies yodelling.
75258.m: In Talerschwingen a spinning coin sings in a bowl.

75259.q: What is the prayer call that alpine herdsmen call out through a milk funnel in the evening?
75259.e: With the Betruf, also called the alpine blessing, the herdsmen ask for protection for people and animals on the alp. The milk funnel amplifies the voice like a megaphone.
75259.m: The Betruf is an old blessing call on the alp.

75260.q: What is the big festival called where yodellers, alphorn players and flag throwers meet every three years?
75260.e: The Federal Yodelling Festival is organised by the Swiss Yodelling Association. It takes place every three years in a different region.
75260.m: The Federal Yodelling Festival takes place every three years.

75261.q: Which small accordion is typical of Swiss folk music?
75261.e: The Schwyzerörgeli is a small diatonic accordion. In many Ländler bands it plays the melody.
75261.m: The Schwyzerörgeli is the typical instrument of Ländler music.

75262.q: What are the large forged bells called that people shake in time during Trychle?
75262.e: Treicheln are forged from sheet metal and have a dull, loud sound. During Trychle, groups walk in step and swing them in rhythm.
75262.m: Treicheln are forged bells used in Swiss customs.

75263.q: What is an alphorn traditionally made of?
75263.e: The alphorn is usually made of spruce wood. Although it is made of wood, it counts as a brass instrument because of its mouthpiece.
75263.m: The alphorn is made of wood.

75264.q: What is the famous herding song from the canton of Fribourg that is sung at the Fête des Vignerons in Vevey?
75264.e: “Le Ranz des vaches” is a cow call in the Fribourg dialect. It recalls the herds being taken up to the alpine pastures.
75264.m: “Le Ranz des vaches” is a famous cow call from Fribourg.

75265.q: What is the subject called in which you learn music mainly through movement?
75265.e: In eurhythmics children experience beat and tempo with their whole body. It was invented by the Geneva music teacher Émile Jaques-Dalcroze.

75266.q: What do children often do to music in a eurhythmics lesson?
75266.e: In eurhythmics children walk, clap and jump to the music. That way they feel beat and tempo in their bodies.
75266.m: In eurhythmics you learn music through movement.

75267.q: Which way does the hand move on the first beat of a bar when conducting?
75267.e: The first beat is shown with a clear downward movement. That way everyone sees the start of the bar at once.
75267.m: When conducting, the first beat goes down.

75268.q: In 3/4 time, which way does a right-handed conductor move for the second beat?
75268.e: In 3/4 time the hand draws roughly a triangle. For the second beat it moves out to the right.
75268.m: In triple time the second beat goes to the right.

75269.q: Using Zoltán Kodály’s method, which rhythm syllable do you say for a crotchet (quarter note)?
75269.e: Kodály used simple syllables so that children can speak and clap rhythms. Two quavers are called “ti-ti”.
75269.m: Rhythm syllables help you speak and feel note values.

75270.q: By how much do two dots to the right of a note lengthen it?
a: By three quarters of its value
By a quarter of its value
75270.e: The first dot adds half the note’s value, the second adds half of that again, so a quarter. Together that makes a half plus a quarter, which is three quarters.
75270.m: A second dot adds half the value of the first dot.

75271.q: How many quavers (eighth notes) does a dotted crotchet last?
75271.e: A crotchet lasts two quavers. The dot adds half, so one quaver: 2 plus 1 makes 3 quavers.
75271.m: A dotted crotchet lasts as long as three quavers.

75272.q: A piece in 4/4 time lasts exactly 32 crotchet beats. How many bars does it have?
75272.e: Each bar of 4/4 contains four crotchet beats. 32 divided by 4 makes 8 bars.
75272.m: You get the number of bars by dividing all the beats by the beats per bar.

75273.q: In the treble clef, which note sits on the top line?
75273.e: The fourth line is D and the top space is E. So the top line above it is F, an octave above the F in the bottom space.
75273.m: The top line in the treble clef is F.

75274.q: In the treble clef, which note sits on the middle line?
75274.e: The third line is exactly in the middle of the stave. In the treble clef the B above middle C sits there.
75274.m: On the middle line of the treble clef sits B.

75275.q: Which group of clefs do the alto and tenor clefs belong to?
75275.e: The centre of the alto and tenor clefs points to the line of middle C. That is why they are called C clefs.
75275.m: The alto and tenor clefs are C clefs.

75276.q: In the bass clef, which note sits on the bottom line?
75276.e: Counting from the bottom in the bass clef, the first line is G and the second line is B.
75276.m: The bottom line in the bass clef is G.

75277.q: Which major key has two flats in its key signature?
75277.e: In B flat major the notes B and E are lowered to B flat and E flat. That is why there are two flats in the key signature.
75277.m: B flat major has the flats B flat and E flat.

75278.q: Which minor key shares its key signature with F major?
75278.e: The relative minor lies a minor third below the keynote of the major key. A minor third below F is D.
75278.m: D minor is the relative minor of F major.

75279.q: Which notes make up the G major triad?
75279.e: Above G, B forms a major third, and above that D forms a minor third. That makes a major triad.
75279.m: The G major triad is made of G, B and D.

75280.q: Which major key, like A minor, has no sharps or flats at all?
75280.e: A minor is the relative minor of C major. Both use only the white keys of the piano and so have no sharps or flats.
75280.m: A minor is the relative minor of C major.

75281.q: What does “subito piano” mean in written music?
75281.e: Subito is Italian for “at once, suddenly”. So the volume changes to quiet without any transition.
75281.m: Subito means that something happens suddenly.

75282.q: What does “decrescendo” mean in written music?
75282.e: Decrescendo means “decreasing” in Italian. The volume falls bit by bit. The opposite is crescendo.

75283.q: What is the dynamic level between piano and mezzo forte called?
75283.e: From quiet to loud the levels are pp, p, mp, mf, f and ff. So mezzo piano (mp) is a little louder than piano.
75283.m: Mezzo piano is a little louder than piano.

75284.q: What does the tempo marking “Moderato” mean?
75284.e: Moderato comes from the Italian word for “moderate”. The tempo is neither slow nor fast.

75285.q: What does the performance marking “rubato” mean?
a: Shaping the tempo freely, with slight changes
Keeping the tempo exactly the same
75285.e: Rubato means “stolen”: you take a little time here and give it back there. It is typical of Romantic piano music.
75285.m: In rubato the tempo can breathe freely.

75286.q: What does the tempo marking “Vivace” mean?
75286.e: Vivace means “lively” in Italian. The tempo is quick and cheerful.

75287.q: What does the tempo marking “Lento” mean?
75287.e: Lento is Italian for “slow”. It is one of the calmest tempo markings.

75288.q: What is the tempo marking for “as fast as possible”, even faster than presto?
75288.e: The ending -issimo means “very” or “most”. So prestissimo is the fastest usual tempo.
75288.m: The ending -issimo makes a tempo marking stronger.

75289.q: What does the tempo marking “Grave” mean?
75289.e: Grave is Italian for “heavy, serious”. It stands for a very slow, weighty tempo.
75289.m: Grave means heavy and very slow.

75290.q: What is the very low female voice, below the normal alto, called?
75290.e: The contralto is the lowest female voice. This voice type is rare.
75290.m: The contralto is the lowest female voice.

75291.q: What is the male voice between baritone and deep bass called?
75291.e: The bass-baritone combines the depth of the bass with the height of the baritone. In opera it often sings roles like Wotan in Wagner.
75291.m: The bass-baritone lies between baritone and bass.

75292.q: What do you call imitating drum sounds using only your mouth, lips and voice?
75292.e: In beatboxing you make bass, snare and hi-hat sounds with your mouth alone. It is an important art form of hip-hop culture.
75292.m: In beatboxing your mouth becomes a drum kit.

75293.q: Which way does the hand move on the last beat of a bar when conducting?
75293.e: The last beat goes up so that the hand can swing back for the next first beat. That is why it is also called the upbeat.
75293.m: When conducting, the last beat of a bar goes up.

75394.q: According to the colour theory you learn at school, how many primary colours are there in the paint box?
75394.e: At school you learn about three primary colours. You can mix many other colours from them.

75395.q: Which colour is a primary colour?
75395.e: Yellow is one of the three primary colours. Green, orange and purple only come about through mixing.

75396.q: Which of these colours is also a primary colour?
75396.e: Blue is a primary colour. Brown, pink and grey are mixed colours.

75397.q: Which primary colour is in both orange and purple?
75397.e: Orange contains red and yellow, and purple contains red and blue. What they both have is red.
75397.m: Red is in orange and in purple.

75398.q: Can you mix a primary colour from other paints?
75398.e: Primary colours cannot be mixed from other colours. That is why they are called primary colours.
75398.m: You cannot mix a primary colour.

75399.q: Which Swiss artist developed a famous colour theory with a colour wheel?
75399.e: Johannes Itten was born in the canton of Bern in 1888. He taught at the Bauhaus in Germany and wrote a well-known book about colours.
75399.m: Johannes Itten was a Swiss colour theorist.

75400.q: Which primary colour do you need for both green and orange?
75400.e: For green you mix yellow with blue, and for orange yellow with red. So both contain yellow.
75400.m: Yellow is in green and in orange.

75401.q: What happens to watercolour paint when you add a lot of water?
75401.e: A lot of water thins the paint. The white paper shows through and the colour looks light.
75401.m: With a lot of water, paint becomes lighter.

75402.q: What kind of green do you get when you mix a lot of yellow with only a little blue?
75402.e: The more yellow there is in the mixture, the lighter and more yellowish the green becomes.
75402.m: With more yellow, green becomes lighter.

75403.q: Which colour do you get from blue and a lot of white?
75403.e: White lightens any colour. So blue becomes a light blue like the sky.
75403.m: White turns blue into light blue.

75404.q: Which colour do you get from red and a little black?
75404.e: Even a little black makes red much darker.
75404.m: Red with black becomes dark red.

75405.q: What is the best colour to start with if you want to mix a light colour?
75405.e: You add the dark colour to the light one in small amounts. The other way round, you need a great deal of paint.
75405.m: Add a little dark to the light colour.

75406.q: Which colour do you get from black and white?
75406.e: Black and white together make grey. The more white, the lighter the grey.

75407.q: What do you usually get when you mix all three primary colours together?
75407.e: If you mix red, yellow and blue, the colour becomes dark and brownish.
75407.m: All the primary colours together become dark and brown.

75408.q: What are colours that you mix from two primary colours called?
75408.e: Green, orange and purple come from two primary colours. They are called secondary colours.
75408.m: Secondary colours come from primary colours.

75409.q: Which season is often painted with cool colours?
75409.e: In winter there is snow and ice. Blue, turquoise and white suit it.
75409.m: Winter is often painted with cool colours.

75410.q: Which group does the colour turquoise belong to?
75410.e: Turquoise lies between blue and green. It looks fresh like sea water.

75411.q: Which colour is considered a cool colour?
75411.e: Blue reminds us of ice and cold water. That is why it counts as a cool colour.

75412.q: What do warm colours often remind us of?
75412.e: Red, orange and yellow look like fire and the sun. That is why they seem warm.
75412.m: Warm colours remind us of fire.

75413.q: What do cool colours often remind us of?
75413.e: Blue and turquoise look like ice and water. That is why they seem cool.
75413.m: Cool colours remind us of ice and water.

75414.q: Which colours are best for painting a crackling campfire?
75414.e: Warm colours suit fire. They glow and look hot.
75414.m: You paint fire with warm colours.

75415.q: Which colours are best for painting a glacier in winter?
75415.e: A glacier is cold. That is why cool colours such as blue and turquoise suit it.
75415.m: You paint ice with cool colours.

75417.q: How does a room painted entirely in red and orange often feel?
75417.e: Red and orange are warm colours. They make a room feel warm.
75417.m: Warm colours make a room cosy.

75418.q: What does a colour wheel show?
75418.e: On the colour wheel, the colours are arranged round in a circle. This shows which colours are related.
75418.m: The colour wheel puts the colours in order.

75419.q: How many colours does Johannes Itten's well-known colour wheel have?
75419.e: Itten's colour wheel has twelve colour fields. They include primary colours, secondary colours and in-between shades.
75419.m: Itten's colour wheel has twelve colours.

75420.q: Which shape do the three primary colours form in the middle of Itten's colour wheel?
75420.e: In the middle of Itten's colour wheel there is a triangle. It is divided into three fields with the three primary colours.
75420.m: In Itten's colour wheel, the primary colours are in a triangle.

75421.q: What are colours that sit right next to each other on the colour wheel called?
75421.e: Neighbouring colours such as yellow and orange sit side by side on the colour wheel. Together they look harmonious and calm.
75421.m: Neighbouring colours sit next to each other on the colour wheel.

75422.q: Which colour is opposite yellow on the colour wheel?
75422.e: Yellow and purple are a pair of opposite colours. They are also called complementary colours.
75422.m: Yellow and purple are opposite colours.

75423.q: What are two colours that face each other on the colour wheel called?
75423.e: Colours opposite each other on the colour wheel are called complementary colours. They are also called opposite colours.

75424.q: Where is orange on the colour wheel?
75424.e: A secondary colour sits on the colour wheel between the colours it is made from.
75424.m: Secondary colours sit between their primary colours.

75425.q: How do two opposite colours look when you paint them next to each other?
75425.e: Opposite colours strengthen each other. That is why they stand out especially next to each other.
75425.m: Opposite colours look very bright next to each other.

75426.q: How does watercolour paint usually change when it dries?
75426.e: Wet paint shines and looks stronger. As it dries, it becomes a little lighter.

75427.q: What should you do before you take a new colour?
75427.e: With a clean brush, the new colour stays nice and clear. Otherwise it gets muddy.
75427.m: Wash out the brush before every new colour.

75428.q: What happens when you paint a lot of water onto the paper?
75428.e: Thin paper soaks up the water and goes wavy. Thick painting paper helps prevent this.
75428.m: Too much water makes paper go wavy.

75429.q: What is the metal part of a paintbrush that holds the hairs in place called?
75429.e: The ferrule is the little metal tube on the brush. It holds the hairs together.
75429.m: The ferrule holds the brush hairs in place.

75430.q: Which brush is good for thin, fine lines?
75430.e: A thin round brush has a fine tip. With it you can paint narrow lines.
75430.m: For fine lines you use a thin brush.

75431.q: What are watercolour paints that look see-through and let the paper show through called?
75431.e: The German word Aquarell comes from the Latin word for water. These paints are thin and translucent.

75432.q: What do you need a cloth for when painting with watercolours?
75432.e: You use the cloth to dab extra water out of the brush.

75433.q: What happens when you dab watercolour paint onto wet paper?
a: It rolls off the paper in drops
75433.e: On wet paper, the paint flows apart softly. This creates soft blends.
75433.m: On wet paper, the paint spreads out.

75434.q: What are wax crayons mainly made of?
75434.e: Wax crayons are made of wax with colour powder mixed into it.
75434.m: Wax crayons are made of wax.

75435.q: What happens to wax crayons when they lie in the hot sun?
75435.e: Wax melts when it is warm. That is why the crayons go soft and can melt.
75435.m: Wax goes soft in the heat.

75436.q: How do you colour a large area quickly with a wax crayon?
a: With the long side of the crayon
75436.e: You take the paper off the crayon and colour with its side. That way the area quickly becomes colourful.
75436.m: You colour large areas with the side of the crayon.

75437.q: You put paper on a leaf and rub over it with a wax crayon. What do you see?
a: A mirror image of the leaf
75437.e: A leaf has fine veins. Rubbing makes them visible on the paper. This technique is called frottage.

75438.q: What happens when you paint over a wax drawing with watercolour?
75438.e: Wax and water do not get on. The watercolour runs off the wax in drops and the drawing stays visible.

75439.q: What do you use to draw a “secret picture” that only appears when you paint over it with watercolour?
75439.e: You can hardly see white wax on white paper. When you paint over it with colour, the picture appears.
75439.m: White wax becomes visible with paint.

75440.q: How do you make a scratch picture with wax crayons?
a: Paint black over a colourful layer, then scratch
Wipe a picture away with water
Tear up paper and glue it
75440.e: First you colour everything brightly, then paint black over the top. When you scratch, the bright colours come through again.
75440.m: In a scratch picture, you scratch the colour free.

75441.q: Why are wax crayons good for small children?
a: They are thick and rarely break
They are as sharp as needles
75441.e: Wax crayons are thick and sturdy. Small hands can hold them well.
75441.m: Wax crayons fit well in small hands.

75442.q: What do you do to paper to give it soft, uneven edges for a collage?
75442.e: Torn paper has a soft, frayed edge. Cut paper has smooth edges.

75443.q: Which language does the word “collage” come from?
75443.e: The French word “coller” means to glue.

75444.q: Which tools do you need most for a collage?
75444.e: You cut out the pieces with the scissors. You stick them on with the glue.
75444.m: For a collage you need scissors and glue.

75445.q: Which material is good for a collage?
75445.e: You can cut pictures and letters out of magazines and stick them on.
75445.m: Old magazines are good collage material.

75446.q: Which famous painter made the first collages together with Georges Braque?
75446.e: Around 1912, Picasso and Braque glued pieces of paper into their pictures. That is how collage became known in art.
75446.m: Picasso was gluing collages early on.

75447.q: Which French artist, in old age, cut colourful shapes out of paper with scissors?
75447.e: Henri Matisse was ill and could hardly paint any more. So he cut out coloured paper shapes and stuck them on.
75447.m: In old age, Matisse painted with scissors.

75448.q: What is the old Swiss art of cutting delicate pictures out of paper called?
75448.e: Paper cutting is especially famous in the Pays-d'Enhaut in the canton of Vaud. It often shows cows being taken up to the Alpine pastures.
75448.m: Paper cutting is a Swiss folk art.

75449.q: Which natural material can you collect in autumn for a collage?
75449.e: In autumn the leaves are red, yellow and brown. Once dried, they are easy to stick on.
75449.m: Autumn leaves are good for collages.

75450.q: What do people often use to make a simple stamp print at school?
75450.e: You cut a pattern into half a potato. Then you put paint on it and press it onto the paper.
75450.m: A potato can be a stamp.

75451.q: How does a letter appear on the paper if it is the right way round on the stamp?
75451.e: When you print, everything is mirrored. That is why you have to cut letters into the stamp back to front.
75451.m: A print is back to front.

75452.q: What do you need a roller for when printing?
75452.e: With the roller you roll the paint thinly and evenly onto the printing block.

75453.q: In lino printing, what do you use to cut the grooves into the soft block?
75453.e: You use a small gouge to cut grooves into the soft linoleum. These parts stay white when you print.
75453.m: In lino printing, you cut with a gouge.

75454.q: Which parts of a potato stamp print colour onto the paper?
75454.e: Only what sticks up touches the paper. The parts cut away stay white.
75454.m: On a stamp, only what sticks up prints.

75455.q: What can you cover with paint and print to show fine veins?
75455.e: You paint a leaf and press it onto the paper. The veins then appear as a fine pattern.
75455.m: A leaf leaves a beautiful print.

75456.q: What must you put on the stamp before every new print?
75456.e: When printing, the stamp passes its paint to the paper. For the next print it needs paint again.
75456.m: Before every print, put new paint on the stamp.

75457.q: How many identical pictures can you print with a monotype?
75457.e: “Mono” means one. A monotype produces just a single print.

75458.q: Which shape has no corners at all?
75458.e: A circle curves all the way round. That is why it has no corners.

75459.q: Which shape has four sides of the same length and four right angles?
75459.e: In a square, all four sides are the same length.
75459.m: A square has four equal sides.

75460.q: What is a line that goes up and down like pointed mountains called?
75460.e: A zigzag line has sharp corners. A wavy line, on the other hand, is soft and round.
75460.m: A zigzag line has sharp points.

75461.q: What is a line that turns inwards like a snail's shell called?
75461.e: A spiral keeps turning around a centre point.

75462.q: What is a line that goes from top to bottom like a flagpole called?
75462.e: A vertical line stands straight up. A horizontal line lies flat like the horizon.
75462.m: Vertical means from top to bottom.

75463.q: Which painter from Russia liked to paint circles, triangles and lines?
75463.e: Wassily Kandinsky is considered a pioneer of abstract art. His pictures often show colourful shapes instead of things.
75463.m: Kandinsky painted with shapes and colours.

75464.q: What is a line made up of lots of little dots called?
75464.e: If you put lots of dots one after another, you get a dotted line.
75464.m: A dotted line is made of dots.

75465.q: What is a picture showing the face of another person called?
75465.e: A portrait shows a person, often only the head and shoulders. If you paint yourself, it becomes a self-portrait.

75466.q: In the past, what did a painter usually need in order to paint a self-portrait?
75466.e: In the mirror, painters see their own face. That way they can copy it.
75466.m: For a self-portrait, you look in the mirror.

75467.q: What is a self-portrait taken with a mobile phone called?
75467.e: A selfie is a photo of yourself. It is a modern form of self-portrait.
75467.m: A selfie is a photo of yourself.

75468.q: Roughly where are the eyes in a drawn face?
a: In the middle of the head
Right at the top of the head
Right at the bottom by the chin
75468.e: Many people think the eyes are high up. In reality, they are at about half the height of the head.
75468.m: The eyes are about halfway down the head.

75469.q: Roughly where are the ears in a drawn face?
a: Between the eyes and the tip of the nose
75469.e: The ears begin at about the height of the eyes and eyebrows. They end at about the height of the tip of the nose.
75469.m: The ears reach from the eyes to the nose.

75470.q: Which painter with a red beard often painted himself, including in a straw hat?
75470.e: Vincent van Gogh had little money for models. That is why he often painted himself.

75471.q: What is different in a mirror compared with reality?
75471.e: In the mirror, your right hand appears as your left hand. That is why self-portraits often show a mirrored face.
75471.m: A mirror swaps left and right.

75472.q: Which German artist painted himself from the front with long curls in 1500?
75472.e: Albrecht Dürer from Nuremberg painted several self-portraits. The picture from 1500 is especially famous.

75473.e: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa in Italy more than 500 years ago.
75473.m: Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa.

75474.q: What colours is the headscarf in Vermeer's “Girl with a Pearl Earring”?
75474.e: The girl wears a blue turban with a yellow cloth. Jan Vermeer was a painter from Holland.
75474.m: Vermeer's girl wears a blue and yellow cloth.

75475.q: What is the “Mona Lisa” especially known for?
75475.e: Many people puzzle over whether the Mona Lisa is smiling or not.

75476.q: What shines in the sky in Vincent van Gogh's painting “The Starry Night”?
75476.e: Van Gogh painted a night sky with swirling, shining stars and a bright moon.
75476.m: Stars and the moon shine in The Starry Night.

75478.q: Where did Michelangelo paint his famous pictures in the Sistine Chapel in Rome?
75478.e: For years, Michelangelo painted high up on scaffolding on the chapel ceiling.

75479.q: What does Edvard Munch's painting “The Scream” show?
a: A figure with its hands on its face
75479.e: The figure holds its hands to its head and has its mouth wide open.
75479.m: The Scream shows a frightened figure.

75480.q: Which mountain can be seen small in the background of Hokusai's picture “The Great Wave”?
75480.e: Behind the huge wave you can see Mount Fuji, small. It is the highest mountain in Japan.
75480.m: Mount Fuji stands behind the Great Wave.

75481.q: Which painter liked to paint mountains, cows and mountain farmers in the Engadine?
75481.e: Giovanni Segantini spent his last years in Maloja in the Engadine. There is a museum with his paintings in St Moritz.
75481.m: Segantini painted life in the Alps.

75482.q: What did Henri Rousseau often paint, even though he had never been there?
75482.e: Henri Rousseau got his ideas from the botanical garden and zoo in Paris. His jungle pictures are full of leaves and animals.
75482.m: Rousseau painted jungles from his imagination.

75483.q: In which village in the canton of Bern was Albert Anker born?
75483.e: Albert Anker was born in Ins in the Seeland. He also died there.

75484.q: In which century did Albert Anker mainly live?
75484.e: Albert Anker lived from 1831 to 1910. That is mainly the 19th century.
75484.m: Albert Anker lived in the 19th century.

75485.q: Who did Albert Anker especially like to paint, and paint often?
75485.e: Albert Anker painted many pictures of children reading, knitting, playing or sleeping.

75486.q: What was Albert Anker supposed to become before he became a painter?
75486.e: Anker was first supposed to become a priest and studied at university for this. Then he decided on art.
75486.m: Anker first wanted to become a priest.

75487.q: Which country did the painter Albert Anker come from?
75487.e: Albert Anker was born in Ins in the canton of Bern. He is one of the best-known painters in Switzerland.
75487.m: Albert Anker was a Swiss painter.

75488.q: Which place often appears in Albert Anker's paintings?
75488.e: Anker painted several pictures of classrooms and school exams, for example “The School Examination”.
75488.m: Anker often painted the village school.

75489.q: Albert Anker did not only paint on canvas. What else did he paint many pictures on?
75489.e: Anker painted many ceramic plates and dishes for a workshop in Paris.

75490.q: What can you visit in Ins today to see where Anker worked?
75490.e: The Anker House in Ins shows his studio just as he used it.
75490.m: The Anker House is in Ins.

75491.q: What did Albert Anker do for a few years alongside painting?
a: He was a politician in Bern
He was a cook in Paris
